[16:03] Martin Vogel (Director of Enterprise Applications, DeltaWorks Manufacturing): That is an honest answer. Most vendors say "yes, it handles that."
[16:09] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): It handles it if you build it to. It doesn't handle it by magic.
[16:15] Anika Bose (IT Governance Lead, DeltaWorks Manufacturing): Can the exception queue be owned by a team rather than a named individual? Our people change roles constantly and individual ownership is one of the reasons our current automations decay.
[16:29] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Yes. Route to a group, resolve a person dynamically from a field, or use an on-call style fallback. Run history persists, so an administrator can see inputs, which steps ran, and where it stopped.
[16:45] Anika Bose (IT Governance Lead, DeltaWorks Manufacturing): And who can see the payload in that history?
[16:49] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Permissions can separate workflow administration from business viewing. Field-level masking for specific payloads is a design conversation rather than a checkbox — I don't want to say "yes, masking" and have you discover the nuance later.
[17:08] Anika Bose (IT Governance Lead, DeltaWorks Manufacturing): I have written "design conversation" three times now.
[17:13] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): [laughs] I know. I'd rather that than three promises.
[17:18] Anika Bose (IT Governance Lead, DeltaWorks Manufacturing): I agree, actually. It is unusual.
[17:22] Martin Vogel (Director of Enterprise Applications, DeltaWorks Manufacturing): Let me ask the SAP question directly, because it is the one that decides this.
[17:29] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Go ahead.
[17:31] Martin Vogel (Director of Enterprise Applications, DeltaWorks Manufacturing): How do you connect to SAP S/4HANA?
[17:35] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): There are a few routes and which one is right depends on your landscape. There are API-based options, there's the generic REST action for anything that exposes a service, and for on-premise components the agent or gateway pattern I mentioned. What I will not do is tell you there's a one-click SAP connector that solves your estate, because your estate is not one thing.
[18:03] Martin Vogel (Director of Enterprise Applications, DeltaWorks Manufacturing): It is definitely not one thing.
[18:06] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): What I'd want, before anyone talks about a pilot, is a list of the specific SAP operations phase one needs. [18:27] Martin Vogel (Director of Enterprise Applications, DeltaWorks Manufacturing): I can produce that list.
[18:30] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): That would change this conversation from architecture in the abstract to architecture with numbers in it.
[18:38] Martin Vogel (Director of Enterprise Applications, DeltaWorks Manufacturing): How long would you need with the list?
[18:41] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): A week, and I'd want an hour with whoever owns your SAP interfaces rather than reading a spreadsheet in isolation.
[18:51] Martin Vogel (Director of Enterprise Applications, DeltaWorks Manufacturing): That can be arranged.
[18:54] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Can I flag something commercial that's hiding in this? If phase one requires significant SAP and on-premise work, that's professional services, and I'd rather price it honestly up front than have it appear after architecture review.
[19:12] Martin Vogel (Director of Enterprise Applications, DeltaWorks Manufacturing): Thank you. That is exactly the thing I was going to raise later.
[19:18] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Then let's raise it now.
[19:21] Martin Vogel (Director of Enterprise Applications, DeltaWorks Manufacturing): The headline licence price is not going to surprise me. We buy enterprise software. What I care about is transparency around professional services, premium connectors, and anything we would only discover after an architecture review. That is where the surprises live.
[19:43] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Then here's what I'll commit to. The proposal will separate licence, assumed builder count, viewer and approver population, expected workflow volume, and services as distinct line items, with the assumptions written next to each. And where I don't know, it'll say "to be determined after architecture review" rather than a placeholder number that looks like a quote.
[20:11] Martin Vogel (Director of Enterprise Applications, DeltaWorks Manufacturing): If you do that, you will be the second vendor this year who has.
[20:17] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Who was the first?
[20:19] Martin Vogel (Director of Enterprise Applications, DeltaWorks Manufacturing): [laughs] I'm not going to tell you that.
[20:23] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Fair enough. For the record — Growth is eighteen hundred a month up to thirty users on an annual agreement, but that's not your shape. You're an Enterprise conversation. Custom priced, advanced governance, security capabilities, higher usage.
[20:42] Martin Vogel (Director of Enterprise Applications, DeltaWorks Manufacturing): Yes, obviously.
[20:45] Anika Bose (IT Governance Lead, DeltaWorks Manufacturing): What is a user? We may have twenty people building and several hundred who only approve something.
[20:53] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Builders and full workspace users are the licensed users. Approval-only or notification-only populations can be structured differently depending on package. I'm not going to give you a number today because without the user model any number is misleading.
[21:12] Anika Bose (IT Governance Lead, DeltaWorks Manufacturing): Please put that in the proposal explicitly. I do not want to discover in year two that every occasional approver requires a full seat.
[21:23] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): It'll be explicit.
[21:26] Martin Vogel (Director of Enterprise Applications, DeltaWorks Manufacturing): There is a second use case I should mention, not for phase one.
[21:32] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Go on.
[21:34] Martin Vogel (Director of Enterprise Applications, DeltaWorks Manufacturing): Replacing several departmental Python scripts with centrally visible automations and approvals. The four-year-old script Anika mentioned is not unique. We think there are — Anika, what was the estimate?
[21:51] Anika Bose (IT Governance Lead, DeltaWorks Manufacturing): We identified thirty-one. We believe there are more.
[21:56] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Thirty-one that you know about.
[21:59] Anika Bose (IT Governance Lead, DeltaWorks Manufacturing): Thirty-one that we know about. Yes.
[22:03] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): That's a genuinely good second-phase use case, and I'd note it's a different kind of value than the first one. The first one is cycle time. This one is risk reduction and auditability.
[22:19] Anika Bose (IT Governance Lead, DeltaWorks Manufacturing): For me it is the more interesting one.
[22:23] Martin Vogel (Director of Enterprise Applications, DeltaWorks Manufacturing): For finance it is the less interesting one, which is why it is phase two.
[22:29] Anika Bose (IT Governance Lead, DeltaWorks Manufacturing): [laughs] That is accurate.
[22:33] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): I'd argue you can put a number on it. Not savings — avoided incident cost. But that's a harder internal sell and I wouldn't lead with it.
[22:45] Anika Bose (IT Governance Lead, DeltaWorks Manufacturing): No. Lead with cycle time.
[22:49] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Environment separation — you'd flagged wanting separate developer, test and production workspaces with change control.
[22:58] Martin Vogel (Director of Enterprise Applications, DeltaWorks Manufacturing): That is not negotiable. We do not put anything into production that has not been through test, and we do not let the person who built something be the only person who approves it.
[23:12] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Workspace separation is supported and Enterprise has stronger governance around who can publish where. There's version history and change metadata on every workflow. Rollback and promotion patterns vary a bit depending on the workflow and the package, and I'd want to walk through your specific promotion process rather than assume it maps.
[23:37] Martin Vogel (Director of Enterprise Applications, DeltaWorks Manufacturing): Our promotion process is documented. I will send it.
[23:42] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Then I'll map it against what the platform does and tell you where the gaps are. There will be gaps — there always are — the question is whether they're gaps you can live with.
[23:56] Anika Bose (IT Governance Lead, DeltaWorks Manufacturing): I would also like the change-management scenario included in any evaluation. Not just "build the workflow." Build it, change it, break it, roll it back.
[24:10] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): That's a better evaluation than most customers design. Yes.
[24:16] Martin Vogel (Director of Enterprise Applications, DeltaWorks Manufacturing): Anika designs our evaluations.
[24:19] Anika Bose (IT Governance Lead, DeltaWorks Manufacturing): Somebody has to.
[24:22] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Can I ask about naming and standards? You mentioned governance of local scripts. What would you want in place before business teams start building?
[24:34] Anika Bose (IT Governance Lead, DeltaWorks Manufacturing): Naming conventions. Change control for anything classified as important. A rule that somebody other than the creator can understand each production workflow. And a register — I want to be able to answer the question "how many automations do we have" without a discovery project.
[24:56] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): That matches our recommended operating model almost exactly. A few centrally owned templates, defined publishing rights, dev separated from prod, and a small central group owning standards while business teams contribute requirements.
[25:15] Martin Vogel (Director of Enterprise Applications, DeltaWorks Manufacturing): Who does that in practice at your other customers? A team? A person?
[25:22] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Usually a small team, two to four people, sitting in whatever function is closest to the process. Sometimes IT, more often operations. The pattern that fails is when it's one person's side project.
[25:39] Martin Vogel (Director of Enterprise Applications, DeltaWorks Manufacturing): We have a lot of one-person side projects.
[25:43] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): I know. That's why I mention it.
[25:47] Anika Bose (IT Governance Lead, DeltaWorks Manufacturing): I have twelve minutes. Can we do the AI question? Because I have a position on it and I would rather state it than have it discovered.
[25:57] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Please.
[26:00] Anika Bose (IT Governance Lead, DeltaWorks Manufacturing): My position is that I do not want generative AI in the first phase at all. Not because I object in principle. Because it adds a review process — data protection, works council, possibly legal — and I do not want that review sitting on the critical path of a project whose value comes from something else entirely.
[26:26] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): That's a strategically sound position and I'm not going to argue with it.
[26:32] Anika Bose (IT Governance Lead, DeltaWorks Manufacturing): I expected you to argue with it.
[26:35] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): The product is a workflow platform. AI steps are optional steps inside a workflow, not the substance of it. If you turn them off, you have a workflow platform. That's fine.
[26:50] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): And to be concrete — Enterprise customers can disable AI features. Administrators can restrict which models are allowed. AI steps are explicit, inspectable workflow steps rather than something ambient. We log the model configuration used on a run. And we don't use customer workflow content to train a shared OrbitFlow model.
[27:16] Anika Bose (IT Governance Lead, DeltaWorks Manufacturing): That last point needs to be contractual.
[27:20] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): It should be, and you should insist on it.
[27:24] Anika Bose (IT Governance Lead, DeltaWorks Manufacturing): I will.
[27:27] Martin Vogel (Director of Enterprise Applications, DeltaWorks Manufacturing): Anika, before you go — is there anything on your list we have not covered?
[27:33] Anika Bose (IT Governance Lead, DeltaWorks Manufacturing): Two things. First, can audit data be exported to our own systems? We do not accept a vendor console as an audit trail.
[27:45] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Run events and metrics through APIs and webhooks, and audit export on Enterprise. Several customers forward failures into their incident tooling.
[27:57] Anika Bose (IT Governance Lead, DeltaWorks Manufacturing): Then that is satisfactory. Second — data deletion. If we terminate, what happens?
[28:06] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): That's a contractual and configuration question and I'd rather it be answered in writing by someone who can commit to it. I'll flag it for the pack.
[28:18] Anika Bose (IT Governance Lead, DeltaWorks Manufacturing): Good. Then I am finished. Martin, you have my notes. Thank you both.
[28:25] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Thank you, Anika. That was genuinely useful.
[28:29] Anika Bose (IT Governance Lead, DeltaWorks Manufacturing): [inaudible] — goodbye.
[28:33] Martin Vogel (Director of Enterprise Applications, DeltaWorks Manufacturing): She is very thorough.
[28:36] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): She's the most organised governance lead I've spoken to this year and I mean that.
[28:43] Martin Vogel (Director of Enterprise Applications, DeltaWorks Manufacturing): She will be pleased. I will not tell her.
[28:47] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): [laughs] Understood.
[28:51] Martin Vogel (Director of Enterprise Applications, DeltaWorks Manufacturing): Can I ask you something slightly off topic?
[28:55] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Of course.
[28:57] Martin Vogel (Director of Enterprise Applications, DeltaWorks Manufacturing): Were you at Hannover Messe in April?
[29:01] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): I wasn't, no. Jon?
[29:04] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): No. I've been to it once, years ago, in a previous job. It is enormous.
[29:11] Martin Vogel (Director of Enterprise Applications, DeltaWorks Manufacturing): It is enormous and it is exhausting. I ask because I spoke to a workflow vendor there and I cannot remember which one, and it has been irritating me for two months.
[29:24] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): If they had an orange stand it wasn't us.
[29:28] Martin Vogel (Director of Enterprise Applications, DeltaWorks Manufacturing): [laughs] I don't remember the colour.
[29:32] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Then it definitely wasn't us. Nobody forgets our stand, we spend far too much on it.
[29:39] Martin Vogel (Director of Enterprise Applications, DeltaWorks Manufacturing): Well. If I remember I will tell you and you can tell me what is wrong with them.
[29:45] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): I'd be delighted.
[29:48] Martin Vogel (Director of Enterprise Applications, DeltaWorks Manufacturing): Shall we do the remaining part? I have until the hour.
[29:53] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Yes. I want to cover ROI, the decision process, and timing, and then I want to ask you a direct question about next steps.
[30:03] Martin Vogel (Director of Enterprise Applications, DeltaWorks Manufacturing): Go.
[30:05] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): ROI. Is this headcount, cycle time, error reduction, or engineering maintenance?
[30:12] Martin Vogel (Director of Enterprise Applications, DeltaWorks Manufacturing): Not headcount. I want to be very clear about that because in a manufacturing business the word automation makes people nervous for reasons that have nothing to do with software.
[30:26] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Understood.
[30:28] Martin Vogel (Director of Enterprise Applications, DeltaWorks Manufacturing): The case is cycle time and error reduction. Catching a data mismatch at contract close instead of in order processing. And there is a maintenance cost that nobody counts — a script takes two days to write and then consumes a few hours every month forever. That never appears in the original estimate.
[30:52] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): We hear that in every industry, and nobody has a number for it.
[30:57] Martin Vogel (Director of Enterprise Applications, DeltaWorks Manufacturing): Because to get the number you have to admit how much time you spend on it.
[31:03] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): [laughs] That's the real reason, isn't it.
[31:07] Martin Vogel (Director of Enterprise Applications, DeltaWorks Manufacturing): It is exactly the reason.
[31:10] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): For a pilot we'd want to baseline one or two measures before automating. Elapsed time, number of manual touches, exception rate, or engineer hours on the current process.
[31:24] Martin Vogel (Director of Enterprise Applications, DeltaWorks Manufacturing): Elapsed time and exception rate. Those we can measure.
[31:29] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): And I'd add adoption. A technically correct workflow that everyone routes around is a failed implementation.
[31:37] Martin Vogel (Director of Enterprise Applications, DeltaWorks Manufacturing): We have a museum of technically correct systems.
[31:41] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): [laughs] Most large companies do.
[31:45] Martin Vogel (Director of Enterprise Applications, DeltaWorks Manufacturing): And the edge cases must be tested, not the average. The business pain is always in the unusual ten percent.
[31:54] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Agreed. Decision process — who's actually involved?
[32:00] Martin Vogel (Director of Enterprise Applications, DeltaWorks Manufacturing): Enterprise applications sponsors, which is me. Then the architecture board, information security, the works council for some workflow monitoring use cases, procurement, and regional IT.
[32:16] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): That's six.
[32:18] Martin Vogel (Director of Enterprise Applications, DeltaWorks Manufacturing): That is six. Welcome to DeltaWorks.
[32:22] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): In what order?
[32:24] Martin Vogel (Director of Enterprise Applications, DeltaWorks Manufacturing): Architecture board first, and that is the one that matters. If architecture says no, nothing else happens. Information security runs in parallel. The works council only if the use case requires it, which is why Anika wanted it discussed today. Procurement last, and slowly.
[32:47] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): And who can say no unilaterally?
[32:51] Martin Vogel (Director of Enterprise Applications, DeltaWorks Manufacturing): Architecture board and information security. Regional IT cannot say no formally but can make implementation impossible, which amounts to the same thing.
[33:04] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): That's a very useful distinction and I appreciate you making it.
[33:09] Martin Vogel (Director of Enterprise Applications, DeltaWorks Manufacturing): I have watched vendors ignore regional IT and I have watched what happens to them.
[33:16] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Noted. Timing?
[33:19] Martin Vogel (Director of Enterprise Applications, DeltaWorks Manufacturing): Formal architecture review in September. Procurement in Q4. Realistic production use early next year.
[33:29] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Early next year.
[33:31] Martin Vogel (Director of Enterprise Applications, DeltaWorks Manufacturing): I know that is slow for you.
[33:34] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): It's slow, but it's honest, and a slow honest timeline is worth more to me than a fast invented one. I've had Q3 dates that turned into the following June.
[33:47] Martin Vogel (Director of Enterprise Applications, DeltaWorks Manufacturing): Ours will not turn into the following June. It may turn into March.
[33:53] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): [laughs] I'll take March.
[33:56] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): What has to be true to move from where we are to a decision?
[34:02] Martin Vogel (Director of Enterprise Applications, DeltaWorks Manufacturing): The architecture has to be viable. Specifically SAP and the on-premise systems. If the answer is "possible but requires nine months of integration work", then the first use case is too heavy and we should choose a different first use case or not proceed.
[34:23] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): That's the crux, isn't it.
[34:26] Martin Vogel (Director of Enterprise Applications, DeltaWorks Manufacturing): That is the crux. Honestly — the biggest issue is whether SAP and our on-premise systems make the implementation too heavy for the first use case. Everything else is manageable.
[34:42] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): And the alternative?
[34:45] Martin Vogel (Director of Enterprise Applications, DeltaWorks Manufacturing): MuleSoft and custom integration services. We already own MuleSoft. If someone can demonstrate that the business-owned workflow layer can be built on top of it acceptably, that is the cheaper path even if it is the worse one.
[35:04] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Is that a real possibility or a procurement position?
[35:09] Martin Vogel (Director of Enterprise Applications, DeltaWorks Manufacturing): [pause] It is a real possibility. I do not think it is a good idea, because it makes every workflow change an integration project, which is the problem we are trying to solve. But it is a real possibility and someone will propose it.
[35:29] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Then let's make sure the architecture note addresses it directly rather than pretending it isn't the alternative.
[35:37] Martin Vogel (Director of Enterprise Applications, DeltaWorks Manufacturing): Yes. Please do that.
[35:40] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Right. Direct question. What's the next step?
[35:45] Martin Vogel (Director of Enterprise Applications, DeltaWorks Manufacturing): I will be honest with you. I see strategic potential here. But I do not think a sandbox is the next step.
[35:54] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Tell me why, because I want to make sure I've understood.
[35:59] Martin Vogel (Director of Enterprise Applications, DeltaWorks Manufacturing): Because a sandbox would show me the product works, and I already believe the product works. It would not tell me whether we can deploy it, and that is the open question. If I give a sandbox to my team they will spend three weeks building something impressive and we will be no closer to knowing whether SAP connectivity is viable.
[36:24] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): That's a completely coherent argument and I'd rather you made it than humoured me.
[36:31] Martin Vogel (Director of Enterprise Applications, DeltaWorks Manufacturing): So — send us the architecture material first. The deployment patterns, the on-premise connectivity options, the SAP integration routes with honest difficulty ratings. Then we determine whether the deployment model is viable. If it is, we talk about a sandbox and a pilot. If it is not, we stop and neither of us has wasted a quarter.
[36:59] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Agreed. Jon, what do you need from Martin to produce that?
[37:05] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): The list of specific SAP operations for the candidate use case. Your promotion process documentation. And an hour with whoever owns the SAP interfaces. With those I can produce something with substance rather than a marketing architecture diagram.
[37:24] Martin Vogel (Director of Enterprise Applications, DeltaWorks Manufacturing): You will have all three by the end of next week.
[37:29] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Then I'll come back within two weeks of receiving them.
[37:34] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): And I'll send the security pack in parallel — SOC 2, subprocessor list, DPA, architecture diagram, retention documentation, DR documentation, pen test material. Plus Jon's note on team-level versus individual-level visibility for the works council question.
[37:56] Martin Vogel (Director of Enterprise Applications, DeltaWorks Manufacturing): Do not forget that note. Anika will ask.
[38:01] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): I won't forget it.
[38:04] Martin Vogel (Director of Enterprise Applications, DeltaWorks Manufacturing): There is one more thing I want to say and then we should finish.
[38:09] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Go ahead.
[38:11] Martin Vogel (Director of Enterprise Applications, DeltaWorks Manufacturing): Some of what we told you today was approximate. The thirty-one scripts is a count from an audit that was not exhaustive. The mismatch cost I could not give you a number for. The two German plants — I said they are prohibited from exposing production databases, and I believe that is correct, but I have not read the actual policy in eighteen months.
[38:38] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): That's exactly the sort of thing I need to know.
[38:42] Martin Vogel (Director of Enterprise Applications, DeltaWorks Manufacturing): So when you write your summary, please separate what we confirmed from what we estimated. I have seen approximations become requirements and then become the reason a project failed.
[38:57] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): I'll send a written recap with open questions in a separate column from confirmed requirements. And I'll list the things I heard as estimates so you can correct them.
[39:11] Martin Vogel (Director of Enterprise Applications, DeltaWorks Manufacturing): Then we understand each other.
[39:14] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Let me summarise. The opportunity is a business-owned workflow layer above MuleSoft, not a replacement for it. The first candidate is contract close to SAP validation to ServiceNow tasks, with early mismatch escalation. The decisive question is deployment architecture, specifically SAP and on-premise connectivity, and until that's answered nothing else matters. Governance requires the full security pack plus a works council position on individual-level visibility. And the next step is architecture material, not a sandbox.
[39:56] Martin Vogel (Director of Enterprise Applications, DeltaWorks Manufacturing): That is an accurate summary. I am mildly surprised.
[40:01] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): [laughs] I'll take mildly surprised.
[40:05] Martin Vogel (Director of Enterprise Applications, DeltaWorks Manufacturing): It is high praise from me.
[40:08] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): One last thing from me, if there's time.
[40:12] Martin Vogel (Director of Enterprise Applications, DeltaWorks Manufacturing): Quickly.
[40:14] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Rate limiting. You mentioned SAP. If there's a downstream quota or a throttling constraint on any of these systems, give me the actual number rather than "it's sensitive to load", because high-volume behaviour should be tested against a real limit.
[40:33] Martin Vogel (Director of Enterprise Applications, DeltaWorks Manufacturing): There is a constraint on one of the SQL Server systems. I will find the number.
[40:40] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Thank you. That's the kind of thing that surfaces in week eight otherwise.
[40:46] Martin Vogel (Director of Enterprise Applications, DeltaWorks Manufacturing): Understood. Right. Thank you both. This was more useful than I expected.
[40:53] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Thank you, Martin. And if you remember the vendor from Hannover, do tell me.
[40:59] Martin Vogel (Director of Enterprise Applications, DeltaWorks Manufacturing): [laughs] I will. Goodbye.
[41:03] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Bye.
[41:05] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Bye.

context.text:
=== CALL-002 (call kind: prospect)
CALL ID: CALL-002
DATE: 2026-06-05
VENDOR: OrbitFlow
PROSPECT: BrightPath Health
INDUSTRY: Digital health
COMPANY SIZE: 1,100 employees
STAGE: Technical discovery
DURATION: 34 minutes
PARTICIPANTS:
- Maya Chen, Account Executive, OrbitFlow
- Jon Bell, Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow
- Priya Shah, Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health
- Elliot Greene, Security Architect, BrightPath Health
TRANSCRIPT
[00:00] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Morning both. Priya, Elliot — thanks for the time.
[00:05] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): Morning. Quick logistics thing before we start. Elliot has a hard stop at forty past. So can we do security first and everything else after he drops?
[00:17] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Absolutely, and honestly that's the right order anyway. If security's a no, the rest is theatre.
[00:25] Elliot Greene (Security Architect, BrightPath Health): I appreciate you saying that. Most vendors want to do the demo first and then act surprised.
[00:33] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): I've been on the wrong end of that. Okay — Elliot, you drive. What's on your list?
[00:41] Elliot Greene (Security Architect, BrightPath Health): Right. The list is: we need to resolve the BAA question, review your subprocessors, SSO and SCIM, understand retention, and confirm how US data is handled.
[00:57] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Which of those is the gate?
[01:01] Elliot Greene (Security Architect, BrightPath Health): The BAA is the gate. If you can't offer one, we cannot use OrbitFlow for any workflow that may involve protected health information. That's not me being difficult, that's — that's just where we are.
[01:19] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Understood, and I want to be careful here because this is exactly the thing people fudge on sales calls. I'm not going to give you a yes on this call. What I will do is get you a written answer from our legal and compliance side within — Jon, what's realistic, a week?
[01:41] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): A week is realistic for a written position, yes.
[01:46] Elliot Greene (Security Architect, BrightPath Health): A written position is fine. A verbal "we're working on it" is not.
[01:52] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Agreed.
[01:55] Elliot Greene (Security Architect, BrightPath Health): Okay. Baseline certifications?
[01:59] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): SOC 2 Type II is the baseline. SAML SSO and SCIM provisioning, both on Enterprise. Encryption in transit and at rest. Audit logs covering administrative and workflow events. Retention configurable within supported ranges. EU data residency available on Enterprise.
[02:22] Elliot Greene (Security Architect, BrightPath Health): EU. We're a US operation with a UK subsidiary. What's the default region?
[02:30] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Default depends on where the workspace is provisioned. I'd rather confirm the specifics in writing than guess at your architecture on a call.
[02:41] Elliot Greene (Security Architect, BrightPath Health): Good. That's the right answer.
[02:45] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): Elliot's tolerance for confident guessing is quite low.
[02:50] Elliot Greene (Security Architect, BrightPath Health): [crosstalk] It's zero. It's zero, Priya.
[02:53] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): [laughs] Noted.
[02:57] Elliot Greene (Security Architect, BrightPath Health): Subprocessors. Do you publish a list, and do you notify on change?
[03:04] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): We publish the list and there's a notification mechanism for changes. The exact notice period is contractual, so — again, that's a document question not a call question.
[03:18] Elliot Greene (Security Architect, BrightPath Health): Fine. Retention. Can I set it, and can I set it differently per workspace?
[03:26] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Configurable within supported ranges. Per-workspace granularity I'd want to check against your specific requirement, because there are limits.
[03:37] Elliot Greene (Security Architect, BrightPath Health): What's the floor?
[03:40] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): I don't want to quote you a number I'd have to walk back. I'll put it in the pack.
[03:47] Elliot Greene (Security Architect, BrightPath Health): Okay.
[03:50] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): Can I add one? Environment separation. We'd want granular separation between sandbox and production — not just a flag, actual separation.
[04:03] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Workspace separation is supported, and Enterprise has stronger governance around who can publish where. What I'd want to understand is whether you mean separate data planes or separate logical workspaces, because those are very different asks.
[04:22] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): Logical is probably enough. Elliot?
[04:26] Elliot Greene (Security Architect, BrightPath Health): Logical is probably enough if the access controls are real and the audit trail crosses both.
[04:34] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): That's supportable.
[04:37] Elliot Greene (Security Architect, BrightPath Health): Now the one I actually care about. What happens to data sent to an LLM provider?
[04:45] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Honest answer, it depends on configuration and provider, so I don't want to over-generalise. We use enterprise API arrangements where those exist, and providers are documented as subprocessors. For customers with stricter policies there are two options — disable AI entirely, or scope the initial phase to deterministic workflow steps and let security review model usage on a separate track.
[05:14] Elliot Greene (Security Architect, BrightPath Health): The second one. That separation would help a lot, actually. AI is interesting but it's not worth blocking the automation use case over.
[05:26] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): That's a bigger concession than you usually make.
[05:30] Elliot Greene (Security Architect, BrightPath Health): I'm aware.
[05:33] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Just so I capture it correctly — AI off for phase one, reviewed separately, not ruled out permanently?
[05:42] Elliot Greene (Security Architect, BrightPath Health): Correct.
[05:45] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): I'll add — AI steps here are explicit, inspectable workflow steps. They're not ambient. Admins restrict which models are allowed, Enterprise can disable the features entirely, and we log the model configuration used on each run. We also don't use customer workflow content to train a shared OrbitFlow model.
[06:09] Elliot Greene (Security Architect, BrightPath Health): That last sentence. Is it in the contract or is it on a marketing page?
[06:15] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): It needs to be in the contract for you to rely on it, and I'd expect you to insist on that.
[06:22] Elliot Greene (Security Architect, BrightPath Health): I will insist on that.
[06:25] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): Write it down, Elliot.
[06:27] Elliot Greene (Security Architect, BrightPath Health): It's written down.
[06:31] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): What else can we send? SOC 2 report, subprocessor list, DPA, architecture diagram, retention documentation — is that the pack?
[06:42] Elliot Greene (Security Architect, BrightPath Health): Add pen test summary. And yes. And we'll send you our questionnaire, which is long, and I apologise in advance.
[06:53] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): They're all long. We'll complete it.
[06:58] Elliot Greene (Security Architect, BrightPath Health): One more. Who at your end can see our run data?
[07:04] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Role-based access, workspace separation, and secrets are never displayed in run logs. Internally, support access is controlled and logged. If you need field-level masking for specific payloads, that's a design conversation rather than a checkbox.
[07:24] Elliot Greene (Security Architect, BrightPath Health): We will need that conversation. We have workflows where an admin should know a step failed without seeing the record contents.
[07:35] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Yeah, that's a very common pattern in your sector. It's designable, I just don't want to say "yes, masking, done" when the real answer is "yes, with design".
[07:48] Elliot Greene (Security Architect, BrightPath Health): Understood. Right, that's most of my list. I've got twenty-five minutes before I have to go. Priya, do you want to do current state so I can hear it?
[08:00] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): Yes, let's.
[08:03] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Please. What's actually broken today?
[08:08] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): Two things, and they're linked. First, business teams request automations from a small systems group — my group — and there's a growing backlog. Second, compliance review slows down any workflow that touches patient-adjacent data, which is most of them.
[08:29] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): How long's the backlog?
[08:32] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): Currently? [pause] I'd say eleven weeks for anything non-trivial. It was six in January.
[08:41] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): So it's getting worse.
[08:44] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): It's getting worse. And what happens when the backlog gets long is people route around us. Someone builds something in Power Automate, it works, they leave, and then it's nobody's.
[08:59] Elliot Greene (Security Architect, BrightPath Health): Which is my problem, eventually.
[09:03] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): Which becomes Elliot's problem, eventually, yes.
[09:07] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Is it that the steps are manual, or —
[09:11] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): No, that's the thing. It's not that every step is manual, we have automation in places. The problem is the gaps between the automated pieces. Something fires, then there's a four-day hole where a human is supposed to notice, and sometimes they don't.
[09:31] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Do you have telemetry on that or is it anecdotal?
[09:36] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): Mix. Outcome metrics exist. Operational telemetry is weak. We can usually tell you something was late after the fact. We're much worse at answering why it was late, or which dependency failed, or whether the same failure happened fifteen times last month.
[09:57] Elliot Greene (Security Architect, BrightPath Health): Can I correct something, actually, before we go further.
[10:02] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): Go on.
[10:04] Elliot Greene (Security Architect, BrightPath Health): I said earlier — and I've said it in other meetings — that patient information never goes into HubSpot. Policy says it shouldn't. In practice we do occasionally find patient names in free-text fields. Which is exactly why I'm strict about the boundary. I don't want you designing against the policy version of our data.
[10:31] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): That's genuinely useful and it's not a small admission.
[10:36] Elliot Greene (Security Architect, BrightPath Health): It's not an admission, it's a control gap I'm managing. But yes.
[10:42] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): [laughs] Sorry.
[10:45] Elliot Greene (Security Architect, BrightPath Health): The process people describe and the process people run are not the same thing. That's true everywhere.
[10:53] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): It is. Okay, let me play the stack back. HubSpot, Microsoft Teams, Azure, Databricks, Jira Service Management.
[11:05] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): That's it. Plus a lot of SharePoint that nobody admits to.
[11:11] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Which is the system of record for the process?
[11:15] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): Depends on the object. Customer and commercial data has a clear home. Tasks and tickets have a different home. [11:36] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): And you've got Power Automate today.
[11:40] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): We do. It's already covered by our Microsoft agreement, which matters a lot to procurement.
[11:48] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): So what's the problem with it?
[11:51] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): Complex flows are difficult to monitor. And ownership becomes unclear when the creator changes role, which happens constantly. So I want to be clear — I'm not sitting here saying we have no automation. The question is whether a different layer gives us better maintainability and operational control.
[12:15] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): That's the right question, and we won't try to replace everything. [12:35] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): That's closer to how we'd think about it. I'd be nervous if the proposal was migrate everything off Microsoft.
[12:44] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): It isn't, and frankly that proposal would lose to your licensing agreement anyway.
[12:51] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): It would.

[13:14] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): That last clause is the important one. Yes, that's a good candidate.

[13:25] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Understood. And that's a real design constraint — you'd want to pass references rather than payloads wherever possible, and only pull the sensitive field at the point of use, if at all.
[13:39] Elliot Greene (Security Architect, BrightPath Health): Yes. Exactly that.
[13:43] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): One caveat on the workflow, though. The happy path is not the hard part.
[13:50] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Go on.
[13:52] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): I want to see what happens when data's missing, when an API times out, when an approver does nothing for two days, when the account changes state after the workflow's already started.

[15:31] Elliot Greene (Security Architect, BrightPath Health): That's what I wanted to hear. If it only lives in your console it's not an audit trail, it's a screenshot.
[15:40] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): [laughs] I'm going to steal that.

[15:54] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): Go ahead.

[16:20] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): That's a fair challenge and I'd want to demo the permission model specifically rather than hand-wave it.
[16:29] Elliot Greene (Security Architect, BrightPath Health): Then let's do that in the next session. Right — I have to go. Priya, you've got my notes. Thanks both.
[16:39] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Thanks Elliot, appreciate the directness.
[16:43] Elliot Greene (Security Architect, BrightPath Health): [inaudible] — thanks.

[17:58] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): Nine days.
[18:00] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Nine days. I still think about it.
[18:04] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): We had something similar with a HubSpot sync. Not nine days. Four. But similar.

[26:40] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): The last one. That's the one my director cares about.
[26:45] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Then that's the baseline.

[29:44] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): I'll hold you to that.
[29:47] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Please do.
[29:50] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): So — where does that leave us. My read is I would still consider a limited pilot with synthetic or clearly non-PHI data. [30:15] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): That's understood and I'd rather you said it now.
[30:20] Priya Shah (Head of Business Systems, BrightPath Health): Good.
[30:23] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Concrete next steps then. We send the security pack — SOC 2, subprocessors, DPA, architecture diagram, retention docs, pen test summary. [04:13] Nina Patel (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): That's a workspace-level governance question and I believe yes, but I want to confirm the exact granularity rather than guess. I'll come back in writing.

[04:27] Noah Williams (VP Operations Technology, Ember Financial): Hannah, what's your actual position? Because in the internal meeting you were more open than this.
[04:35] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): My position is that deterministic workflow steps are not a model risk problem and I'd support those tomorrow. Generative steps in a decision path are a nine-month problem. Generative steps that produce a summary a human reads, where the human makes the decision — that's a grey area and I'd want to argue it case by case.
[04:58] Nina Patel (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): That grey area is where most of the value is, for what it's worth.
[05:03] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): I know. That's why it's worth arguing about rather than banning.
[05:09] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Can I note something for the record — the second use case Noah sent through was using AI to summarise incidents for operations leaders, without allowing sensitive records to train external models. Is that in the grey area or over the line?
[05:26] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): Grey. A summary for a human reader is defensible. What's not defensible is if that summary silently becomes the input to something automated later.
[05:39] Nina Patel (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Then the design principle is that the AI output is a leaf node, not an intermediate value. It gets rendered to a person, it doesn't feed the next branch.
[05:52] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): [pause] Yes. That's — yes, that's the right way to put it. Can you enforce that or is it a convention?
[06:01] Nina Patel (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Today it's a design convention plus review, not a hard platform constraint. I'm not going to tell you there's a switch labelled "AI outputs cannot feed decisions", because there isn't.
[06:15] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): Thank you. That's useful and it's a real gap.
[06:20] Nina Patel (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): It is a real gap. I'll feed it back.
[06:24] Noah Williams (VP Operations Technology, Ember Financial): Auditability, Hannah.
[06:27] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): Right. The list is: SOC 2, SSO and SCIM, exportable audit history, retention controls, encryption details, subprocessor review, EU residency for European records, and contractual language that our data is not used to train shared AI models.
[06:49] Nina Patel (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): SOC 2 Type II is the baseline. SAML SSO and SCIM on Enterprise. Encryption in transit and at rest. Retention configurable within supported ranges. EU data residency available on Enterprise. Run events and metrics through APIs and webhooks, and audit export on Enterprise. And we don't use customer workflow content to train a shared OrbitFlow model.
[07:17] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): The last one — contractual or marketing?
[07:21] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): It needs to be contractual for you to rely on it, and I'd expect legal to insist.
[07:28] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): They will.
[07:30] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): On exportable audit history — define exportable. Because I've had vendors mean "you can download a CSV from a UI" and that is not exportable.
[07:43] Nina Patel (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): [laughs] API and webhook based, so programmatic. Several customers forward failures and audit events into their own tooling continuously rather than pulling reports. That's the pattern I'd recommend for you.
[07:59] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): Into our SIEM.
[08:01] Nina Patel (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Into your SIEM, yes.
[08:04] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): Then that's satisfactory, subject to seeing the actual payload schema.
[08:10] Nina Patel (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): I'll send the schema.
[08:13] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): Good. That's my two gates addressed at the level a call can address them.
[08:20] Noah Williams (VP Operations Technology, Ember Financial): Then let's do the use case, because I want Nina to see how ugly it is.
[08:26] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Please.
[08:28] Noah Williams (VP Operations Technology, Ember Financial): High-value operational exceptions are currently handled through Slack channels and custom scripts. That's the whole architecture. Someone posts in a channel, someone else picks it up, a script does part of it, and there's a spreadsheet.
[08:46] Nina Patel (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): And the problem is auditability.
[08:49] Noah Williams (VP Operations Technology, Ember Financial): The problem is auditability and the problem is that four engineers hold the whole thing in their heads. If two of them left in the same quarter we'd be in genuine difficulty.
[09:03] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): Three of them are on the same team.
[09:06] Noah Williams (VP Operations Technology, Ember Financial): Three of them are on the same team, yes, which is worse.
[09:11] Nina Patel (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Do you have telemetry on how often exceptions occur and how long they take?
[09:17] Noah Williams (VP Operations Technology, Ember Financial): Partially. We have outcome metrics. Operational telemetry is weak — we can usually tell you something was late after the fact. We're much worse at answering why, or which dependency failed, or whether the same pattern happened fifteen times last month.
[09:37] Nina Patel (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): And the Slack channel is unsearchable in practice.
[09:42] Noah Williams (VP Operations Technology, Ember Financial): It's searchable. It's not auditable. Those are different things and an auditor made that point to us fairly forcefully last year.
[09:53] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): That's actually what started this project.
[09:57] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Can I ask what the auditor said? If you're able to share.
[10:02] Noah Williams (VP Operations Technology, Ember Financial): The polite version was that our exception handling process was "not evidenced."
[10:09] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): The impolite version was longer.
[10:12] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): [laughs] I can imagine.
[10:15] Nina Patel (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Okay. So let me play back the phase-one candidate as I understood it. Detect failed or delayed partner onboarding events. Enrich them from Salesforce and Snowflake. Open a Jira incident. And maintain a complete audit trail of approvals and remediation steps.
[10:36] Noah Williams (VP Operations Technology, Ember Financial): That's it. The last clause is why we're here.
[10:41] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): The last clause is the entire project.
[10:45] Nina Patel (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Then let me show you how a run is recorded rather than how a workflow is built, because I think that's what you actually want to see.
[10:55] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): Yes.
[10:57] Nina Patel (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Sharing. [pause] Can you see it?
[11:02] Noah Williams (VP Operations Technology, Ember Financial): Yes.
[11:04] Nina Patel (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): So this is run history. Filter by workflow, status, time, or a business field. I'll open a run — and you get every step, its inputs, its outputs, timing, retries, and any human approval with who approved and when.
[11:23] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): Can I see one that failed and was remediated?
[11:28] Nina Patel (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): [pause] This one. So it timed out on the external call, retried twice, went to the exception queue, a human picked it up, modified a value, approved, and it resumed. And all of that is one record.
[11:46] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): The human modified a value.
[11:49] Nina Patel (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Yes.
[11:51] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): Is the original value retained?
[11:54] Nina Patel (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): [pause] You can see both here — the value at the point the step ran and the value after the approval form. So yes, but I want to be precise: that's because this approval was configured to collect a structured input. If someone had just clicked approve, there'd be nothing to compare.
[12:16] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): So it depends on how the workflow was designed.
[12:20] Nina Patel (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): It depends on how the workflow was designed.
[12:24] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): Then design standards matter as much as the platform.
[12:29] Nina Patel (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): For your use case, yes, considerably.
[12:33] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): [pause] I appreciate you not overselling that.
[12:38] Noah Williams (VP Operations Technology, Ember Financial): Hannah has been oversold to a lot.
[12:41] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): I have been oversold to a great deal.
[12:45] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Can I flag something? If design standards are load-bearing for your audit position, that should be a pilot deliverable, not an afterthought. As in, the pilot produces a documented standard for how audit-relevant workflows must be built, and that's a deliverable you keep whether or not you buy.
[13:07] Noah Williams (VP Operations Technology, Ember Financial): That's a good idea.
[13:10] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): That's a very good idea, actually.
[13:13] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Then let's write it into the criteria.
[13:17] Nina Patel (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Let me show the composition point since it came up at the start. [pause] Rather than one large canvas, you build subflows — partner lookup, enrichment, approval, incident creation — and assemble them. So when something fails, you're debugging a twelve-step subflow, not step forty of sixty.
[13:41] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): Can I unit test a subflow?
[13:44] Nina Patel (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): You can run one in isolation with a given input, yes. Whether that meets your definition of a unit test is a different question, and I suspect it doesn't quite.
[13:57] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): It doesn't quite. But running in isolation is most of what I want.
[14:04] Nina Patel (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Can I ask what your engineers found hardest in the Tray PoC? Specifically. Because if it's the debugging loop I want to be tested on that, and if it's something else I'd rather know.
[14:19] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): It's the debugging loop and it's error handling. Retry semantics were opaque. We couldn't always tell whether something had run twice.
[14:31] Nina Patel (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Idempotency.
[14:33] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): Idempotency. Yes.
[14:36] Nina Patel (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): That's a genuinely hard problem and I'm not going to claim we solve it for you. Each run keeps state, retries are visible in the run record, and you can see whether a step executed. But if a downstream system isn't idempotent and you retry a write, you can absolutely create a duplicate. The mitigation is design — idempotency keys, checks before writes — and it's the same mitigation anywhere.
[15:07] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): That's the answer I'd give.
[15:10] Nina Patel (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Then we agree on the problem, which is a start.
[15:15] Noah Williams (VP Operations Technology, Ember Financial): Can I move us to the stack? Because we're at fifteen minutes and I want to cover integrations.
[15:22] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Go.
[15:24] Noah Williams (VP Operations Technology, Ember Financial): Salesforce, Snowflake, Slack, Okta, Jira, and an internal event bus. Required: all of those, plus webhooks and a generic REST connector.
[15:37] Nina Patel (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): The internal event bus — what is it?
[15:41] Noah Williams (VP Operations Technology, Ember Financial): Kafka, effectively. It's Kafka with a wrapper somebody wrote.
[15:47] Nina Patel (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Is it reachable from outside your network?
[15:51] Noah Williams (VP Operations Technology, Ember Financial): Not currently.
[15:53] Nina Patel (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Then that's the one to design for. The others are a mix of native connectors and API options, and I'd validate each required operation in a pilot rather than pointing at logos. The event bus is a real architecture question — probably a gateway or an agent pattern, possibly you publish to a webhook endpoint from your side instead. I'd want an hour with whoever owns it.
[16:20] Noah Williams (VP Operations Technology, Ember Financial): That can be arranged.
[16:23] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): What about schema changes? We've had integrations fail because someone renamed a field and nothing surfaced.
[16:31] Nina Patel (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): We cache metadata but refresh it, and mapping errors surface on the run. For high-impact flows I'd recommend explicit validation at the start rather than assuming every source field is populated. And you can alert when error rates cross a threshold.
[16:51] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): I'd want that tested in the evaluation. With bad data.
[16:56] Nina Patel (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Please give us bad data. Genuinely, the pilots that go wrong are the ones run on clean data.
[17:04] Noah Williams (VP Operations Technology, Ember Financial): We have plenty of bad data.
[17:07] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): [crosstalk] We have exceptional bad data.
[17:10] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): [laughs]
[17:12] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): One thing I want to revisit, actually, before we go further.
[17:17] Noah Williams (VP Operations Technology, Ember Financial): Go on.
[17:19] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): I said in the internal session that all approvals have to remain in Jira. I want to soften that. For low-risk approvals I could imagine keeping them in OrbitFlow, if the audit export is strong enough. I'd want risk to define the boundary rather than have a blanket rule.
[17:41] Noah Williams (VP Operations Technology, Ember Financial): That's a change of position.
[17:44] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): It's a refinement. A blanket rule is easier to enforce and worse for the business. If the audit trail is genuinely exportable and genuinely complete, the location of the approval matters less than the evidence of it.
[18:01] Nina Patel (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): That's a more sophisticated position than most risk functions take.
[18:07] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): Don't flatter me, I'll get suspicious.
[18:10] Nina Patel (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): [laughs] Noted.
[18:13] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Can I make sure I've captured it correctly, though, because it changes scope. Approvals in OrbitFlow are acceptable for low-risk cases subject to audit export quality, with risk tiering to be defined. High-risk approvals remain in Jira.
[18:32] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): That's accurate. And "to be defined" means by us, not by you.
[18:38] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Understood.
[18:41] Noah Williams (VP Operations Technology, Ember Financial): Environment separation — can we have separate dev and production?
[18:47] Nina Patel (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Workspace separation is supported, and Enterprise has stronger governance around who can publish where. There's version history and change metadata on every workflow, so you can see what changed and when. Rollback and promotion patterns vary a bit by package.
[19:07] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): I'd want a change-management scenario in the evaluation. Build it, change it, break it, roll it back. Not just build it.
[19:18] Nina Patel (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): That's a better evaluation than most people design.
[19:23] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): It's the one that finds the problems.
[19:26] Noah Williams (VP Operations Technology, Ember Financial): Can the exception queue be owned by a team rather than a named person? Ours currently isn't and that's part of the four-engineers problem.
[19:37] Nina Patel (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Yes. Route to a group, resolve a person dynamically from a field, or use an on-call style fallback.
[19:46] Noah Williams (VP Operations Technology, Ember Financial): On-call style. Does that integrate with PagerDuty or is it internal?
[19:52] Nina Patel (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): There's an internal fallback mechanism, and separately you can call out to your incident tooling. Which one you'd want depends on whether the exception is an operational incident or a business exception, and I'd argue those should be handled differently.
[20:11] Noah Williams (VP Operations Technology, Ember Financial): They should. We currently handle them identically, which is part of the problem.
[20:18] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Shall I do commercials? Because I want to leave time for next steps.
[20:23] Noah Williams (VP Operations Technology, Ember Financial): Go on.
[20:25] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Growth is eighteen hundred a month up to thirty users on an annual agreement. You're not a Growth shape — you're Enterprise, which is custom priced and adds the advanced governance, the security capabilities, and higher usage.
[20:42] Noah Williams (VP Operations Technology, Ember Financial): The range is roughly where I expected an enterprise workflow product to land. That's not my concern.
[20:50] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): What is?
[20:52] Noah Williams (VP Operations Technology, Ember Financial): Usage overages. If the bill becomes unpredictable as volumes grow, finance will dislike it even if the base price is fine. I've been through this with two other vendors and both times the second-year invoice was the problem, not the first.
[21:12] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): That's the right thing to worry about and I'd rather deal with it now. Usage is scoped on workflow runs and premium connector needs. What I'd want to do is model your actual expected volumes, agree what happens above the threshold before you sign, and put the overage mechanism in the contract explicitly rather than in a rate card that changes.
[21:38] Noah Williams (VP Operations Technology, Ember Financial): Can you cap it?
[21:40] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): There are mechanisms. I don't want to promise a specific structure on a call before I've modelled your volumes, because if I say "yes we can cap it" and then the cap has conditions, I've made things worse.
[21:56] Noah Williams (VP Operations Technology, Ember Financial): Fine. Model it.
[21:59] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): I'll need volume estimates. Exception counts, expected run counts, and how those scale with partner growth.
[22:08] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): We can produce those. They'll be estimates.
[22:12] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Estimates are fine as long as we label them as estimates in the proposal.
[22:18] Noah Williams (VP Operations Technology, Ember Financial): What counts as a user, incidentally? Because we'd have forty builders and up to three hundred people who only approve or view workflow status.
[22:29] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Builders and full workspace users are the licensed users. Approval-only or notification-only populations can be structured differently depending on the package. Forty and three hundred is a very common shape and it's exactly why I won't quote you a number before I know it.
[22:49] Noah Williams (VP Operations Technology, Ember Financial): Make that split explicit in the proposal. I don't want to find out in year two that every approver needs a full seat.
[22:58] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): It'll be itemised.
[23:01] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): Three hundred is optimistic, by the way. It might be more.
[23:06] Noah Williams (VP Operations Technology, Ember Financial): It's three hundred today.
[23:09] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): It's three hundred today.
[23:12] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Then I'll model three hundred and five hundred and you can see the shape of the curve rather than a point estimate.
[23:20] Noah Williams (VP Operations Technology, Ember Financial): That would be genuinely useful.
[23:24] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): How are you making the ROI case internally?
[23:28] Noah Williams (VP Operations Technology, Ember Financial): Not headcount. I want to be clear about that — I'm not going to sell this as a reduction, partly because it isn't true and partly because it would poison adoption before we started. The case is consistency, auditability, and reducing key-person dependency.
[23:49] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): And the audit finding. Which has a cost attached that finance understands very well.
[23:57] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Does it have a number?
[24:00] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): It has a remediation programme, which has a budget, which is a number. Yes.
[24:07] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Then that's your business case and it's a strong one.
[24:12] Noah Williams (VP Operations Technology, Ember Financial): It is, provided we don't over-claim. If we say this solves the audit finding and it only solves eighty percent of it, we're in a worse position than if we'd said eighty.
[24:26] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): We say eighty.
[24:28] Noah Williams (VP Operations Technology, Ember Financial): We say eighty.
[24:31] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): For a pilot we'd want to baseline something before automating. Elapsed time, manual touches, exception rate, or engineer hours on the current process.
[24:43] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): Engineer hours. That's the four-people problem quantified.
[24:49] Noah Williams (VP Operations Technology, Ember Financial): And adoption. A technically correct workflow that everyone routes around is a failed implementation, and our engineers are perfectly capable of routing around things.
[25:02] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): We have a history.
[25:05] Nina Patel (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Can I add one? Test the edge cases rather than average time. In your world the average exception is boring and the interesting ten percent is where the audit risk lives.
[25:19] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): Yes. Precisely.
[25:22] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Timing?
[25:24] Noah Williams (VP Operations Technology, Ember Financial): Technical bake-off in July. Vendor decision in August. First controlled production workflows in October.
[25:33] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): That's tight.
[25:35] Noah Williams (VP Operations Technology, Ember Financial): It's tight but it's real. The remediation programme has a date attached to it and that's what's driving the timeline.
[25:45] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Then let me ask directly. What has to be true for you to choose us over Tray?
[25:52] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): Debugging and audit trail. If your run history is genuinely better to work with, and the audit export is genuinely programmatic, that's the difference. Connector breadth is a tie.
[26:08] Noah Williams (VP Operations Technology, Ember Financial): And I'd add — the honest comparison isn't just Tray. It's also "keep the scripts and document them better." That's cheaper and it's what someone will propose.
[26:22] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Would that satisfy the auditor?
[26:25] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): [pause] No.
[26:28] Noah Williams (VP Operations Technology, Ember Financial): Hannah's pause was the answer.
[26:31] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): It wouldn't satisfy the auditor. But it would be proposed, and somebody senior would find it attractive, and we'd spend two months on it.
[26:42] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Then let's address it in the pilot criteria explicitly rather than pretending the only alternative is Tray. I'd rather we lose to a documented decision than lose to a two-month detour.
[26:57] Noah Williams (VP Operations Technology, Ember Financial): Agreed.
[27:00] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): So where does that leave us?
[27:03] Noah Williams (VP Operations Technology, Ember Financial): Assuming the security material lines up, I want to move. Send sandbox access and a written proposal for a six-week pilot so we can compare it against Tray properly rather than impressionistically.
[27:20] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Six weeks. Starting when?
[27:23] Noah Williams (VP Operations Technology, Ember Financial): As soon as the sandbox exists and Hannah's had the security pack for long enough to complain about it.
[27:31] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): I'll need a week.
[27:33] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Then let's say the pack goes out tomorrow, sandbox by end of next week, pilot starts the week after.
[27:42] Noah Williams (VP Operations Technology, Ember Financial): That works.
[27:44] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Let me list what we owe you. Security pack — SOC 2, subprocessor list, DPA, architecture diagram, retention documentation, encryption details. The audit event payload schema for Hannah. A written answer on per-workspace AI disablement granularity. Sandbox access. And a six-week pilot proposal with three to five success criteria that we write jointly, not that I write and you approve.
[28:15] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): Add the note about AI outputs not being enforceable as leaf nodes. I want that written down as a known limitation, not remembered from a call.
[28:27] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Yes. That goes in as a known limitation.
[28:31] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): Thank you.
[28:34] Nina Patel (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): And I'd like an hour with whoever owns the event bus, and I'd like bad data.
[28:41] Noah Williams (VP Operations Technology, Ember Financial): You'll have both.
[28:44] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): What do you need from us on the commercial side before the pilot?
[28:49] Noah Williams (VP Operations Technology, Ember Financial): Nothing binding. But I'd like the overage modelling done in parallel rather than after, because if the economics don't work at scale I'd rather know in week two than week six.
[29:04] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Understood. I'll need those volume estimates from you.
[29:09] Noah Williams (VP Operations Technology, Ember Financial): You'll have them Friday.
[29:12] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Then let me summarise. You're running a two-horse bake-off with a real third option of doing nothing better. Your gates are model risk and auditability, and the deciding factors against Tray are debugging experience and genuinely programmatic audit export. The timeline is driven by a remediation programme with a fixed date. And a successful pilot means a documented workflow design standard as well as a working workflow.
[29:46] Noah Williams (VP Operations Technology, Ember Financial): That's accurate.
[29:49] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): One correction. It's not a two-horse bake-off, it's a two-horse bake-off where one horse has a six-week head start.
[29:59] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): [laughs] Understood. Thank you for being clear about it.
[30:04] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): I'd rather you knew.
[30:07] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): I'd much rather know. Right — anything else before we drop?
[30:13] Noah Williams (VP Operations Technology, Ember Financial): One thing, and it's not a question. When you send the proposal, please don't send me a forty-slide deck. Send me the pilot criteria, the commercials with assumptions, and the known limitations. That's it.
[30:31] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Three documents, no deck.
[30:34] Noah Williams (VP Operations Technology, Ember Financial): Three documents, no deck.
[30:37] Leo Grant (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Done. Thanks both, this was a good call.
[30:42] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): It was better than the last one we had. Thanks.
[30:47] Nina Patel (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Thanks. And send the bad data, I mean it.
[30:52] Hannah Cole (Senior Risk Engineer, Ember Financial): [laughs] You'll regret that.
[30:55] Noah Williams (VP Operations Technology, Ember Financial): Bye.

answer.summary: This is an inference from the call, not a commitment: Ember Financial is leaning toward OrbitFlow only if it can beat Tray.io on debugging and programmatic audit export, and if the pilot/security material checks out. Noah asked for a six-week OrbitFlow pilot and a written proposal, which is a positive signal, but Hannah’s correction makes clear Tray has a six-week head start. Overall, OrbitFlow looks plausible but not yet likely to beat Tray without a strong pilot result.

question: Are Inkwell Learning's account-health scores reliable enough to drive the at-risk workflow?

penalties_hit.reason: The answer opens with a flat 'No' and concludes the scores shouldn't drive the workflow. It reports neither the internal disagreement nor the fact that the signal is still untested.

correct_reason: The answer flatly declares the scores unreliable, which hits the penalty on the main point. It also leaves out two required facts: the disagreement between Olivia and Darren, and the untested signal with its planned backtest.

verdicts.reason: Only Darren's view is given. Olivia's view that the scores are directionally useful isn't mentioned, and neither is Darren's 'noise with a trend' line.
The answer says Darren later called the 'fewer than half' figure an impression, not a measurement.
The answer says machine-generated usage and structured ticket data should be weighted, with human-maintained fields shown only as context.
The answer doesn't say the signal is untested or mention Darren's backtest of past escalations.
