context.text:
=== CALL-009 (call kind: prospect)
CALL ID: CALL-009
DATE: 2026-08-04
VENDOR: OrbitFlow
PROSPECT: Inkwell Learning
INDUSTRY: Education technology
COMPANY SIZE: 520 employees
STAGE: Solution evaluation
DURATION: 31 minutes
PARTICIPANTS:
- Maya Chen, Account Executive, OrbitFlow
- Jon Bell, Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow
- Olivia Grant, SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning
- Darren Wu, Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning
TRANSCRIPT
[00:00] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Hi Olivia, hi Darren. Olivia, I know you've got a hard stop at half past so I'll keep us moving.
[00:08] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): Thank you. I do, unfortunately.
[00:11] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): I can stay on after if it's useful.
[00:14] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): That'd be helpful, actually. Where I'd like to start is the use case, because we've had two rounds of email on it and I want to make sure we're solving the same problem.
[00:26] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): Yes. So — support volume spikes around school-term launches. Enormously. And the problem isn't the volume itself, we can staff for volume. The problem is that we struggle to distinguish isolated tickets from account-level implementation risk until the escalation reaches an executive.
[00:49] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): So by the time you know, it's already senior.
[00:53] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): By the time I know, a school district's chief of staff has emailed our CEO. That's the current detection mechanism and it is not a good one.
[01:05] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): How often?
[01:07] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): Four or five times a term. Which sounds small until you remember each one is a renewal at risk.
[01:16] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): Can I complicate this before we go further?
[01:20] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): Go ahead, he's going to anyway.
[01:23] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): [laughs] I am. So — the proposal, as I understand it, is to combine Zendesk ticket patterns, Salesforce account status, and Snowflake product usage to flag accounts needing proactive intervention, and create structured follow-up tasks.
[01:41] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): That's how I've written it down, yes.
[01:44] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): Right. And my concern is not whether that's technically possible. It obviously is. My concern is data quality. If Salesforce fields are stale, an elegant workflow will still make bad decisions. Beautifully, consistently, at scale.
[02:04] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): That's a fair challenge and I'd rather have it now.
[02:09] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): There's a specific version of it, actually, and I want to challenge something Olivia said in the last session.
[02:16] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): Here we go.
[02:18] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): Olivia talks about account-health scores as though they're reliable. Leadership uses them, they're on the QBR deck, they're in the board pack. But fewer than half our CSMs update the underlying fields consistently. So I would not treat those scores as ground truth, and if we build a workflow that keys off them we've automated a guess.
[02:44] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): [pause] That's — I don't entirely disagree.
[02:49] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): You've disagreed before.
[02:52] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): I've disagreed with the framing. I think the scores are directionally useful and you think they're noise.
[03:00] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): I think they're noise with a trend in them, which is not the same as useful.
[03:07] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Can I ask a question that might be helpful here?
[03:11] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): Please.
[03:13] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Of the three data sources — Zendesk tickets, Salesforce status, Snowflake usage — which one do you both actually trust?
[03:23] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): [immediately] Snowflake.
[03:25] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): [crosstalk] Snowflake, yes.
[03:27] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): Because it's machine-generated. Nobody has to remember to update it.
[03:33] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): And Zendesk?
[03:35] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): Reasonably good. Ticket volume and category are reliable. The sentiment tagging is not, because it's manual.
[03:45] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): And Salesforce.
[03:47] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): Salesforce is reliable for the commercial facts — contract dates, ARR, owner. It is unreliable for anything a human has to remember to type.
[04:00] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): That's actually a very clean answer and I think it's the design.
[04:06] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): Say more.
[04:08] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Weight the signals by how they're produced. Machine-generated usage data and structured ticket data carry the flag. Human-maintained fields are context you show to the person, not inputs the logic depends on.
[04:26] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): [pause] That's — yes. That's the right architecture.
[04:32] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): Would that actually have caught the escalations we've had?
[04:37] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): That's the question, isn't it.
[04:40] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Can you test it? You've got history.
[04:44] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): How would we test it?
[04:47] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Take the escalations that reached you and run them backwards. For each one, look at what the usage data and ticket data looked like three weeks earlier. If the signal was there, you've got a case. If it wasn't, you've saved yourself a project.
[05:05] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): We could do that with SQL. We don't need a workflow platform to do that.
[05:11] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): You absolutely don't, and you should do it before you buy anything from us.
[05:17] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): [pause] Alright. That's not the answer I expected.
[05:22] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): If the signal isn't in the data, we can't manufacture it. And I'd rather you found that out with a query than with a pilot.
[05:32] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): Darren, could you do that?
[05:35] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): I could do that in a day. Maybe two.
[05:39] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): Then why haven't we?
[05:41] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): Because nobody's asked me to, and because I've been arguing about the health scores instead.
[05:48] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): [laughs] Fair.
[05:51] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): I'd suggest making it the first thing, honestly. It's the cheapest way to find out whether this project should exist.
[05:59] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): I'm slightly surprised you're saying that.
[06:03] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): If it turns out the signal isn't there, you'd discover it in month three of a pilot and I'd have burned your goodwill and my quarter. I'd rather know in week one.
[06:16] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): Alright. Darren, do it.
[06:19] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): I'll do it.
[06:21] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Can I ask what you'd look for? Because the answer isn't binary.
[06:26] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): Meaning?
[06:28] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Meaning it's rarely "the signal was there" or "it wasn't." It's usually "it was there for six of the twelve, and for four of those it was there so early it'd have been indistinguishable from noise."
[06:43] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): That's a good point. So I'd want the lead time as well as the presence.
[06:50] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): And the false positive rate. How many accounts looked the same and turned out fine.
[06:57] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): [pause] Yes. That's the harder half.
[07:02] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): Why harder?
[07:04] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): Because to measure false positives I need to know which accounts were fine, and "fine" isn't recorded anywhere. Absence of escalation isn't the same as fine.
[07:17] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): No, it isn't.
[07:20] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): For what it's worth, that's a problem you'd have with any approach, including buying Gainsight properly. It's not an OrbitFlow problem.
[07:31] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): Speaking of which. You should know what we've got.
[07:35] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Go on.
[07:37] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): Customer success uses a limited Gainsight deployment. Limited meaning we bought it, we implemented about forty percent of it, and then the person who owned it left.
[07:51] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): And my team has built a set of Looker alerts. Which work, but they're alerts. They tell you something and then nothing happens.
[08:02] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): So neither gives you the cross-system workflow.
[08:07] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): Neither gives us the workflow. Gainsight has the customer success concepts but we haven't implemented them. Looker has the data but no ability to make anything happen. And nothing joins Zendesk to Snowflake to Salesforce in a way that produces an action.
[08:28] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Is expanding Gainsight the real alternative?
[08:32] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): It's the alternative someone will propose, yes.
[08:36] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): It's the alternative I'd propose if the cost comparison favoured it.
[08:42] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Then let's do that comparison honestly rather than pretending it isn't the competition.
[08:49] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): I'd want that. A cost model comparing this with expanding Gainsight. Including the implementation effort on both sides, because the forty-percent thing wasn't a licensing failure, it was an implementation failure.
[09:06] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): That's a genuinely useful distinction and I'll build the comparison that way.
[09:12] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): You'll build a comparison that includes your competitor fairly?
[09:17] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): I'll build one that includes them accurately. Whether it's fair is for you to judge, and you should check my numbers.
[09:26] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): [laughs] Alright.
[09:29] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Shall I show something? Because there's a shape here I want to check with Darren.
[09:35] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): Go on.
[09:37] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Sharing. [pause] So this is a workflow that's roughly the pattern we're describing. It's scheduled rather than event-driven — it runs daily, queries the warehouse, joins against the CRM, and evaluates a set of conditions.
[09:56] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): Where does the query live?
[10:00] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): In the workflow, in this case. But you can also point at a view you own in Snowflake, which for you is probably better.
[10:10] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): Much better. I don't want business logic living in two places.
[10:16] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Then the pattern is: you own the definition of "at risk" as a view in Snowflake, we consume it and act on it. The intelligence is yours, the orchestration is ours.
[10:30] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): [pause] That's the first time a vendor has said that to me.
[10:35] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): It's the only version that survives contact with a BI team.
[10:40] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): It really is.
[10:43] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): What does "act on it" mean concretely?
[10:47] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): In this flow — create a structured follow-up task with the account, the signal that triggered it, and links back to the underlying tickets and usage. Assign it to the account's CSM, or to a queue if the owner field is stale. Escalate if nothing happens in N days.
[11:09] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): The escalation. That's the bit I want.
[11:13] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): And it's the bit that's usually missing. An alert with no escalation path is a notification, and notifications get ignored.
[11:23] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): They do. I've got a Slack channel full of them.
[11:28] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): That's my channel and I take that personally.
[11:32] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): [laughs] It's not personal, it's just full.
[11:36] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Can the escalation go to a team rather than a named person? Because "assign to CSM" breaks the moment someone changes role.
[11:47] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): That happens constantly.
[11:50] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Then route to a group, resolve dynamically from a field, or use an on-call style fallback. And run history persists so you can see the inputs, which steps ran, and where it stopped.
[12:04] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): What happens when the workflow makes a bad call? Flags something that's fine.
[12:11] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): That's a good question and the honest answer is you need a feedback path or the thing degrades. If a CSM dismisses a flag, that dismissal should be recorded, and you should look at dismissal rates as a health metric for the workflow itself.
[12:29] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): Does the platform do that or do we build it?
[12:33] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): You build it. It's a field on the task and a report. I'm not going to tell you there's a built-in model-monitoring feature, because there isn't.
[12:44] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): Thank you.
[12:46] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): Why does everyone thank them for saying no?
[12:50] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): Because it's rare.
[12:52] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): [laughs] We get that a lot.
[12:56] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): What about the second thing? The weekly narrative summary.
[13:01] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): That's the AI use case. As I've got it written: produce a weekly narrative summary of emerging customer themes, with links back to supporting tickets and account records.
[13:14] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): Yes. Because I currently get a spreadsheet and I don't read it.
[13:20] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): I make that spreadsheet.
[13:22] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): I know. I'm sorry.
[13:25] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): It's fine, I don't read it either.
[13:28] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): [laughs] Well, that's clarifying.
[13:32] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): The links back are the important part and I'm glad you specified them. The way we'd build it is that the source references are stored alongside the generated output, so whoever reads the summary can click through to the tickets that produced each claim.
[13:51] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): Because otherwise it's just a plausible paragraph.
[13:56] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Otherwise it's a plausible paragraph, yes. And plausible paragraphs are exactly what these models are best at, which is the problem.
[14:06] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): Can it say "I don't know"? If there isn't a theme this week, will it invent one?
[14:13] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): It will if you let it. You can design against that — require a minimum number of supporting tickets before a theme is reported, and route thin cases to review rather than publishing them. What I wouldn't do is rely on the model's own confidence score as a guarantee. The better control is evidence plus workflow policy.
[14:38] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): Meaning the workflow refuses, not the model.
[14:42] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Meaning the workflow refuses. Yes.
[14:46] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): That's a meaningful distinction and most people blur it.
[14:51] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): Can we see the prompt?
[14:53] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Yes. AI steps are explicit, inspectable workflow steps — you can see the prompt, the model, the configuration. Administrators can restrict which models are allowed, and Enterprise customers can disable AI features entirely. We log the model configuration used on each run, and we don't use customer workflow content to train a shared OrbitFlow model.
[15:19] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): That last one matters for us.
[15:22] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): I'd assumed it would. Which brings us to security, and I'd like to hear your list.
[15:29] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): Darren, you've got it.
[15:32] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): SSO, audit logs, retention controls, and a clear boundary around student-level data. That last one is the important one.
[15:43] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Tell me what "clear boundary" means in practice.
[15:47] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): FERPA. We handle data about students in US school districts. Student-level records are subject to specific protections and our position is that they should never leave our warehouse.
[16:03] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): So the workflow operates on account-level aggregates only.
[16:09] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): Correct. Usage counts, engagement rates, ticket volumes at the account level. Never a student record, never a student identifier.
[16:20] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): That's very cleanly specifiable, and it's the sort of constraint that's much easier to enforce if you define it in the Snowflake view rather than in our workflow.
[16:33] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): [pause] Because then it's impossible rather than forbidden.
[16:38] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Because then it's impossible rather than forbidden. If the view we consume contains no student-level columns, no workflow can leak them regardless of who builds it.
[16:51] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): That's the design. That's exactly the design.
[16:56] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): Is that a FERPA answer or an engineering answer?
[17:01] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): It's an engineering answer that makes the FERPA answer easy. Our counsel would much rather hear "the data never leaves" than "the vendor has controls."
[17:14] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): I'd note that we should still complete your security review properly. Making the data question moot doesn't remove the vendor assessment.
[17:24] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): No, but it makes it a normal one rather than a special one.
[17:29] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): On the rest of your list — SOC 2 Type II baseline, SAML SSO and SCIM on Enterprise, encryption in transit and at rest, audit logs covering administrative and workflow events, retention configurable within supported ranges. Run events and metrics through APIs and webhooks, audit export on Enterprise.
[17:53] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): That's sufficient for us. We're not a bank.
[17:57] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): We are occasionally treated like one by district procurement.
[18:02] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): True. Some districts have their own questionnaire.
[18:07] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Would we need to complete those?
[18:10] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): Possibly, for the larger ones. Not for a pilot.
[18:15] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Good to know it's coming, though.
[18:18] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): I've got about ten minutes. Can we do money?
[18:23] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Yes. Growth is eighteen hundred a month up to thirty users on an annual agreement. Enterprise is custom priced and adds the advanced governance, the security capabilities, and higher usage.
[18:38] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): I think the price is reasonable if it lets us consolidate several manual programmes.
[18:45] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Which programmes?
[18:47] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): The spreadsheet Darren makes. The at-risk review meeting, which is ninety minutes a week of expensive people reading a list. And a chunk of what we're notionally paying Gainsight for.
[19:03] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): Olivia, we're not going to switch off Gainsight.
[19:07] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): I know we're not going to switch it off. I'm saying the spend is questionable.
[19:13] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): The spend is very questionable. But that's a separate fight.
[19:19] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): It's a related fight.
[19:22] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): [pause] It's a related fight.
[19:25] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): I'd rather not be in the middle of it, but I'd note that a cost model comparing us with expanding Gainsight will inevitably surface it.
[19:36] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): Which is why I want the model to be honest. If the answer is "expand Gainsight, it's cheaper", I want to be able to say that.
[19:46] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Then say it. I'd rather lose that way.
[19:50] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): What counts as a user?
[19:53] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Builders and full workspace users are the licensed ones. Approval-only or notification-only can be structured differently by package. For you the shape matters — how many people build versus how many receive a task?
[20:10] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): Building? Darren's team, so three or four. Receiving tasks — every CSM, so about sixty.
[20:19] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): Sixty-two.
[20:21] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): Sixty-two.
[20:23] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Then that split goes in the proposal explicitly with the assumptions next to it. I won't quote a figure today because without that split any figure I give would mislead you in one direction or the other.
[20:38] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): Please do make it explicit. I don't want to find out in month four that all sixty-two need full seats.
[20:46] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): It'll be itemised — assumed builders, task recipients, expected run volume, and any one-time services separately.
[20:56] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): Thank you.
[20:58] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): How would you make the ROI case?

[21:16] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): That's the argument, and it's a good one, but it relies on the counterfactual. We'd need to be able to say the intervention caused the renewal, and we can't.
[21:29] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): Nobody can ever say that.
[21:32] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): Which is why finance is sceptical of customer success business cases generally.
[21:38] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Is there a leading indicator you could commit to instead? Something measurable that isn't the renewal itself.
[21:47] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): Such as?
[21:49] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Time from first signal to first intervention. That's measurable, it's attributable, and it's the thing the system actually changes. Whether earlier intervention improves renewal is a separate hypothesis, and honestly it's one you already believe or you wouldn't have a customer success team.
[22:11] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): [pause] That's a better framing than the one we've been using.
[22:16] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): It is. Write that down.
[22:19] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): I'm writing it down.
[22:22] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): And I'd add — Inkwell wants to measure whether the system identifies at-risk accounts earlier than the current process. That's the actual success criterion and it's testable against history.
[22:37] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): Which brings us back to Darren's backward-looking analysis.
[22:42] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): Everything brings us back to that.
[22:45] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): It's the load-bearing question.
[22:48] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): Decision process, quickly, because I need to go. I sponsor it. Darren validates the data architecture — and given the last twenty minutes, that's not a formality. IT security and finance approve. And customer success leadership will judge usability, which is a soft gate but a real one.
[23:11] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Who can say no?
[23:13] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): Darren can effectively say no. Security can say no. Finance can say not yet, which is the same thing in practice.
[23:24] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): I wouldn't say no out of principle. I'd say no if the data doesn't support it.
[23:31] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): I know. That's why you're on the call.
[23:35] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Timing?
[23:37] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): We want a pilot before the November renewal planning cycle, with a decision by late September. That's driven by the calendar rather than by us — if we miss November, the next natural point is March.
[23:54] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): So late September is a real date.
[23:58] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): It's a real date. And term starts in early September, which means everyone in customer success is unavailable for the first two weeks.
[24:09] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): Which means August is the month.
[24:12] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): August is the month, and it's the fourth today.
[24:17] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Then let's not spend two weeks arranging things. What's the fastest useful next step?
[24:24] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): Darren's analysis, obviously.
[24:27] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): I can have that by the end of next week.
[24:31] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): And if the signal is there?
[24:34] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): Then I want to pilot it. [24:56] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): That's the best-specified pilot anyone's proposed to me this year.
[25:02] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): Is that flattery?
[25:04] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): No, it's relief. Most pilots are "build something and we'll see how we feel."
[25:11] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): We don't have time to see how we feel.
[25:15] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Twenty escalations. Can you get the data as it was at the time, or only as it is now?
[25:23] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): [pause] That's a very good question.
[25:27] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): It's the one that breaks backtests.
[25:30] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): Snowflake, yes — we have history, I can reconstruct point-in-time. Zendesk, mostly. Salesforce, no. Salesforce fields get overwritten, there's no history on most of them.
[25:47] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Which is convenient, in a way, because you've already said the Salesforce human-maintained fields shouldn't carry the flag.
[25:56] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): [laughs] That's true. The data limitation and the design decision agree with each other.
[26:04] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): That's the most encouraging thing I've heard today.
[26:08] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): It's coincidence.
[26:10] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): I'll take it.
[26:13] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): Right, I have to go. Maya, what do you owe us?
[26:18] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): The security pack — SOC 2, subprocessor list, DPA, architecture diagram, retention documentation. The cost model comparing us with expanding Gainsight, including implementation effort on both sides. And a written recap separating what you confirmed today from what you estimated.
[26:41] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): What did we estimate?
[26:43] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Four or five escalations a term. Fewer than half of CSMs updating fields consistently. Ninety minutes a week on the review meeting. Sixty-two CSMs was firm, the rest were approximate.
[26:59] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): The "fewer than half" is an impression, not a measurement.
[27:04] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Then it goes in the estimates column, and it's probably worth measuring since it affects the design.
[27:12] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): It's worth measuring regardless.
[27:15] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): Add it to your list.
[27:18] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): My list is getting long.
[27:20] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): [laughs] Thanks both. Genuinely useful. Darren, stay on if you've got questions.
[27:28] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Thanks Olivia.
[27:30] Olivia Grant (SVP Customer Experience, Inkwell Learning): Bye.
[27:33] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): Right. Two things I didn't want to raise in front of her.
[27:38] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Go on.
[27:40] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): First — if we do this, the workflow logic has to be in version control somehow. Or at least reviewable. I'm not having business-critical logic that only exists in a web UI.
[27:55] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Version history and change metadata are there, so you can see what changed and when. Definitions can be exported through the API. Whether that satisfies you as version control depends on what you mean — it's not a git integration.
[28:12] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): It's not git.
[28:14] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): It's not git. I'm not going to pretend it is.
[28:18] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): Can I diff two versions?
[28:21] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): You can see change metadata and version history in the product. A true side-by-side diff of two workflow definitions — I'd want to confirm what the export gives you rather than promise a diff experience.
[28:36] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): Add it to the written list.
[28:39] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Adding it.
[28:41] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): Second thing. What happens when I leave?
[28:45] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): [pause] Are you leaving?
[28:48] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): No. But the last person who owned Gainsight left and that's why we implemented forty percent of it. I want to know that if I get hit by a bus, someone else can pick this up.
[29:03] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): That's the right question and it's mostly not a product answer. The product parts are: workflows built as small readable subflows rather than one enormous canvas, version history so someone can see what changed, and run history so someone can see what actually happens. The rest is your operating model — naming conventions, a rule that someone other than the builder can understand each production flow, documentation as a deliverable rather than a hope.
[29:36] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): So the answer is "it depends on us."
[29:40] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Largely, yes. What I'd say is that this platform makes it possible. It doesn't make it happen.
[29:48] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): That's the honest answer.
[29:51] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): If I told you the tool solves organisational memory I'd be lying to you.
[29:57] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): People have.
[29:59] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): I'm sure.
[30:02] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): Alright. I'll do the backward analysis and I'll be honest about what it shows. If the signal's not there I'll say so and we'll stop.
[30:13] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): That's all I'd want.
[30:16] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): And if it is there, I'll be more enthusiastic than I've been today.
[30:22] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): You've been fine. Sceptical isn't unfriendly.
[30:26] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): [laughs] My last three managers would disagree.
[30:31] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Thanks Darren. Good luck with the query.
[30:35] Darren Wu (Director of Business Intelligence, Inkwell Learning): Thanks. Bye.
[30:37] Jon Bell (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Bye.

So the transcript points away from using Inkwell’s account-health scores to drive the workflow.

correct_reason: The main metrics for each customer are right, but the Pinewood alert-mailbox fact is missing and the Halberd onboarding figure is wrongly credited to OrbitFlow.

verdicts.reason: States 22 workflows (up from 6) and error rate 1.4% down from 4.1%, plus the 40-minute median time; April is not mentioned.

result.question: In the renewal calls only, what reliability or health metrics did OrbitFlow report for each customer?

context.text:
PER-CALL FINDINGS (each call was read on its own for this question; quotes verified)
CALL-011 (Lumen Retail Group): OrbitFlow reported a healthy-but-stretched account: more production workflows and lower error rates, plus a much faster depot-exceptions turnaround, but also clear capacity pressure from repeated run overages and some dormant seats. The main quantified health/reliability points were operational performance metrics, not a formal SLA score.
   [00:23] Ruth Adeyemi: "You're fourteen months in. Twenty-two workflows in production, up from six"
   [00:23] Ruth Adeyemi: "Run volume's roughly two hundred and eighty thousand a month."
   [00:43] Ruth Adeyemi: "Error rate's sitting at one point four percent, which is down from four point one"
   [01:10] Ruth Adeyemi: "Median time from exception raised to first action is now forty minutes."
   [02:03] Ruth Adeyemi: "You've exceeded your contracted run volume in four of the last six months."
   [02:03] Ruth Adeyemi: "June was twenty-two percent over."
   [04:12] Ruth Adeyemi: "You've got nine builders licensed and four of them haven't published anything in six months."
CALL-012 (Pinewood Insurance): OrbitFlow reported several health/reliability signals for Pinewood Insurance: usage had dropped about 40% since March, 6 of 14 production workflows had not run successfully in the last 90 days, one workflow had been failing every four hours since January, and support usage was low/odd with 11 tickets raised this year, 4 closed by the customer themselves. These were presented as evidence of account risk, though some were caveated as not being proactively monitored and low ticket volume can be misleading.
   [00:17] Ruth Adeyemi: "Usage has dropped about forty percent since March."
   [01:58] Ruth Adeyemi: "You've got fourteen workflows in production. Six of them haven't run successfully in the last ninety days."
   [02:33] Ruth Adeyemi: "It's been failing since January. Every four hours."
   [03:10] Ruth Adeyemi: "Not proactively at your account tier, no."
   [14:25] Nadia Rahman: "We've raised eleven tickets this year. Four of them we closed ourselves"
   [15:13] Ruth Adeyemi: "Low ticket volume can mean two things, yes."
CALL-013 (Halberd Security): OrbitFlow reported the account as healthy: usage was healthy, all six builders were active, and the error rate was under one percent. This was stated firmly as part of the renewal summary, not as a tentative estimate.
   [00:24] Ruth Adeyemi: "You're renewing in November, usage is healthy, six builders all active, error rate under one percent"
   [00:36] Grace Okonkwo: "That's fine."

=== CALL-011 (call kind: renewal)
CALL ID: CALL-011
DATE: 2026-09-02
VENDOR: OrbitFlow
CUSTOMER: Lumen Retail Group
INDUSTRY: Grocery retail
COMPANY SIZE: 3,200 employees
STAGE: Renewal / QBR
DURATION: 21 minutes
PARTICIPANTS:
- Ruth Adeyemi, Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow
- Maya Chen, Account Executive, OrbitFlow
- Fiona Bright, Head of Retail Operations, Lumen Retail Group
- Devan Shah, Platform Manager, Lumen Retail Group
TRANSCRIPT
[00:00] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Morning both. So this is the quarterly review and it's also the renewal conversation, which I've merged because I didn't think either of you wanted two meetings.
[00:11] Fiona Bright (Head of Retail Operations, Lumen Retail Group): Correct.
[00:13] Devan Shah (Platform Manager, Lumen Retail Group): [crosstalk] Very correct.
[00:15] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Maya's here for the commercial part. She'll be quiet until then, allegedly.
[00:21] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Allegedly.
[00:23] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Right. Let me start with numbers and then you tell me what I've missed. You're fourteen months in. Twenty-two workflows in production, up from six at the end of the first quarter. Run volume's roughly two hundred and eighty thousand a month.
[00:41] Devan Shah (Platform Manager, Lumen Retail Group): That sounds about right.
[00:43] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Error rate's sitting at one point four percent, which is down from four point one when you started. Most of that improvement came in April.
[00:53] Devan Shah (Platform Manager, Lumen Retail Group): April was when we fixed the store-data validation. That was our fault, not yours.
[01:00] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): I know, but it counts.
[01:03] Fiona Bright (Head of Retail Operations, Lumen Retail Group): What I care about is the depot exceptions workflow. Can you give me that one specifically?
[01:10] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Yes. Median time from exception raised to first action is now forty minutes. It was — Devan, what was it before?
[01:20] Devan Shah (Platform Manager, Lumen Retail Group): Between two and six hours, depending on who was on.
[01:24] Fiona Bright (Head of Retail Operations, Lumen Retail Group): Six hours was optimistic.
[01:27] Devan Shah (Platform Manager, Lumen Retail Group): [laughs] Six hours was the number we admitted to.
[01:31] Fiona Bright (Head of Retail Operations, Lumen Retail Group): That's the one that's changed how the depots work. Genuinely. I had a depot manager tell me in July that he'd stopped keeping his own spreadsheet, and that's — you don't get that often.
[01:47] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): That's the metric I'd actually put in front of your board, for what it's worth. Not the run counts.
[01:54] Fiona Bright (Head of Retail Operations, Lumen Retail Group): I already have.
[01:57] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Good. Now the less pleasant part of the numbers.
[02:02] Devan Shah (Platform Manager, Lumen Retail Group): Overages.
[02:03] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Overages. You've exceeded your contracted run volume in four of the last six months. June was twenty-two percent over.
[02:13] Devan Shah (Platform Manager, Lumen Retail Group): We knew. We've been watching it.
[02:16] Fiona Bright (Head of Retail Operations, Lumen Retail Group): Were we charged for those?
[02:19] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): You were charged for two of them. Two were waived — one in March because it was a retry storm caused by a Salesforce outage on their side, and one in May which I waived because you'd flagged it to us proactively before the invoice.
[02:37] Fiona Bright (Head of Retail Operations, Lumen Retail Group): I didn't know that.
[02:39] Devan Shah (Platform Manager, Lumen Retail Group): I knew about March. I didn't know about May.
[02:43] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): May was a judgement call. I'd rather tell you now than have it look like a discovery in the renewal.
[02:51] Fiona Bright (Head of Retail Operations, Lumen Retail Group): Appreciated. But it does mean the run tier is wrong.
[02:56] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): The run tier is wrong, yes. Which is most of what I want to talk about.
[03:02] Devan Shah (Platform Manager, Lumen Retail Group): Can I ask something before we get to money?
[03:06] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Go on.
[03:08] Devan Shah (Platform Manager, Lumen Retail Group): The retry storm in March. Has anything changed at your end so that doesn't happen again? Because from our side we did nothing wrong and it cost us twenty thousand runs.
[03:22] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Partly. There are retry controls and you can set caps per workflow, and we can look at whether yours are configured sensibly — I suspect two or three of them aren't. But if a downstream system is down for six hours and your workflows keep firing, you will burn runs.
[03:43] Devan Shah (Platform Manager, Lumen Retail Group): So the answer is configure it better.
[03:47] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): The answer is configure it better, and I should have done that with you in April rather than now. That's on me.
[03:56] Devan Shah (Platform Manager, Lumen Retail Group): [pause] Alright.
[03:58] Fiona Bright (Head of Retail Operations, Lumen Retail Group): Can we book that as a session rather than an action item that dies?
[04:04] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Yes. I'll put an hour in with Devan for the fortnight after next.
[04:10] Devan Shah (Platform Manager, Lumen Retail Group): Fine.
[04:12] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Adoption. This is the bit I want to push on. You've got nine builders licensed and four of them haven't published anything in six months.
[04:23] Devan Shah (Platform Manager, Lumen Retail Group): Two of those have moved teams.
[04:26] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Then we should take them off, not keep paying for them.
[04:31] Fiona Bright (Head of Retail Operations, Lumen Retail Group): You're offering to reduce our seat count?
[04:34] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): I'm telling you what the data says. Maya may have a different view.
[04:40] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): I have exactly the same view. Nine licensed builders with four dormant is a renewal that gets scrutinised. I'd rather sell you seven active seats and a higher run tier than nine seats where four are indefensible.
[04:57] Fiona Bright (Head of Retail Operations, Lumen Retail Group): That's — okay. That's a more sensible conversation than I was braced for.
[05:04] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Braced for what?
[05:06] Fiona Bright (Head of Retail Operations, Lumen Retail Group): Braced for "here's a fifteen percent uplift, sign here."
[05:11] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): There is an uplift. I'll come to it.
[05:15] Fiona Bright (Head of Retail Operations, Lumen Retail Group): [laughs] Of course there is.
[05:18] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Let me finish the review first, because there's an expansion question and I think it changes the shape of the commercial conversation.
[05:27] Fiona Bright (Head of Retail Operations, Lumen Retail Group): Go on.
[05:29] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): You mentioned in July you were thinking about the supplier onboarding process.
[05:35] Fiona Bright (Head of Retail Operations, Lumen Retail Group): Devan, do you want to?
[05:37] Devan Shah (Platform Manager, Lumen Retail Group): So — at the moment, bringing on a new supplier involves about nine handoffs between buying, compliance, finance and the depot systems team. It's email and a SharePoint list.
[05:52] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): How long?
[05:54] Devan Shah (Platform Manager, Lumen Retail Group): Target's fifteen working days. Actual is somewhere around thirty.
[05:59] Fiona Bright (Head of Retail Operations, Lumen Retail Group): Thirty-four last quarter.
[06:02] Devan Shah (Platform Manager, Lumen Retail Group): Thirty-four. And the buying team is now blaming compliance and compliance is blaming the depot systems team, and honestly they're all a bit right.
[06:13] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Is that a workflow problem or an organisational problem?
[06:18] Devan Shah (Platform Manager, Lumen Retail Group): [pause] That's a good question.
[06:21] Fiona Bright (Head of Retail Operations, Lumen Retail Group): It's both, but I'd say the reason it's an organisational problem is that nobody can see where it's stuck. If you could see it, the arguing would stop.
[06:33] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): That's usually true. I'd flag one risk though — if the process itself is genuinely broken, automating it makes it a faster broken process.
[06:45] Devan Shah (Platform Manager, Lumen Retail Group): We've said that internally.
[06:48] Fiona Bright (Head of Retail Operations, Lumen Retail Group): Compliance said it, and they said it loudly.
[06:52] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Then I'd suggest the first phase is visibility only. Don't automate the handoffs. Just instrument them — track where a supplier onboarding is, who has it, how long they've had it. Run that for six weeks and look at the data.
[07:11] Fiona Bright (Head of Retail Operations, Lumen Retail Group): And then automate.
[07:13] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): And then automate the bits the data says are actually the problem, rather than the bits people complain loudest about. Those are usually different.
[07:24] Devan Shah (Platform Manager, Lumen Retail Group): That's cheaper too.
[07:26] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): It's cheaper and it's much easier to get compliance to agree to.
[07:31] Fiona Bright (Head of Retail Operations, Lumen Retail Group): [pause] Yes. Let's do that.
[07:35] Devan Shah (Platform Manager, Lumen Retail Group): Would that be a lot of runs?
[07:38] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): No. Instrumentation is light — you're recording state transitions, not orchestrating them. Maybe a few thousand a month.
[07:48] Devan Shah (Platform Manager, Lumen Retail Group): That's nothing.
[07:50] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): It's nothing. The expensive phase is later.
[07:54] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Which is relevant to how I structure the renewal, actually.
[07:59] Fiona Bright (Head of Retail Operations, Lumen Retail Group): Go on then. Let's do it.
[08:02] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Right. Current contract is Enterprise, nine builder seats, run tier at two hundred and fifty thousand a month. It expires the eighteenth of October.
[08:14] Fiona Bright (Head of Retail Operations, Lumen Retail Group): Six weeks.
[08:16] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Six weeks, which is why I wanted this conversation now rather than in October.
[08:22] Fiona Bright (Head of Retail Operations, Lumen Retail Group): What's the uplift?
[08:24] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): List uplift at renewal is seven percent. That's the standard annual adjustment and I'm not going to pretend it's negotiable in principle — it applies to everyone.
[08:36] Fiona Bright (Head of Retail Operations, Lumen Retail Group): Seven. Not fifteen.
[08:39] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Seven.
[08:41] Fiona Bright (Head of Retail Operations, Lumen Retail Group): That's more reasonable than I expected.

[11:14] Grace Okonkwo (Chief Information Security Officer, Halberd Security): That's not a control, that's a culture.
[11:17] Tobias Lund (VP Service Delivery, Halberd Security): It's a culture that's worked.
[11:20] Grace Okonkwo (Chief Information Security Officer, Halberd Security): It's a culture that works until someone's on holiday and someone else is in a hurry.
[11:26] Nina Patel (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Can I suggest the lightest version? You don't need a full dev-test-prod pipeline for six people. What you need is that publishing to production requires a second person, and that there's version history so you can see what changed. The version history exists already.
[11:45] Tobias Lund (VP Service Delivery, Halberd Security): Does it? I've never looked at it.
[11:48] Nina Patel (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Version history and change metadata on every workflow. You can see what changed and when and by whom.
[11:56] Tobias Lund (VP Service Delivery, Halberd Security): [pause] Right. That's useful.
[12:00] Grace Okonkwo (Chief Information Security Officer, Halberd Security): How have you been operating this for eighteen months without knowing that?
[12:05] Tobias Lund (VP Service Delivery, Halberd Security): Because nothing's broken, so I've never needed to look.
[12:10] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Which is fair, but it's also the reason I raise it now rather than after something breaks.
[12:17] Grace Okonkwo (Chief Information Security Officer, Halberd Security): Can we require two-person publishing?
[12:20] Nina Patel (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Enterprise supports governance around who can publish where, so the mechanism is separating build permissions from publish permissions. Whether there's a formal two-person approval gate specifically — that's the same permissions question I'm already checking. I'll fold it into the same answer.
[12:41] Grace Okonkwo (Chief Information Security Officer, Halberd Security): Five written answers now.
[12:44] Nina Patel (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Five.
[12:46] Grace Okonkwo (Chief Information Security Officer, Halberd Security): You're very willing to say "I'll check."
[12:50] Nina Patel (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): I'd rather be slow and right. Especially with you.
[12:55] Grace Okonkwo (Chief Information Security Officer, Halberd Security): [laughs] Especially with me, yes.
[12:59] Tobias Lund (VP Service Delivery, Halberd Security): Can I raise one thing that isn't on the agenda?
[13:03] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Go on.
[13:05] Tobias Lund (VP Service Delivery, Halberd Security): We've had two people ask about a mobile experience. Analysts who want to approve something from a phone at two in the morning.
[13:15] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): What's the honest answer, Nina?
[13:18] Nina Patel (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): The web experience works on a phone in the sense that it renders. It is not a mobile product and I wouldn't sell it as one. If your analysts need to approve at two in the morning from a phone, that's going to be a poor experience.
[13:35] Tobias Lund (VP Service Delivery, Halberd Security): Is there a workaround?
[13:37] Nina Patel (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): The approval could be surfaced somewhere they already are. Teams or Slack — a notification with the context and an action, rather than a link into our UI.
[13:49] Tobias Lund (VP Service Delivery, Halberd Security): We're in Teams.
[13:51] Nina Patel (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Then that's the pattern. It's more design work than clicking a setting, but it's the right answer and it'd work better than a mobile app would.
[14:02] Tobias Lund (VP Service Delivery, Halberd Security): Can you scope that?
[14:04] Nina Patel (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): I'll include it in what I send. Rough shape, not an estimate.
[14:10] Grace Okonkwo (Chief Information Security Officer, Halberd Security): Two in the morning approvals worry me slightly.
[14:14] Tobias Lund (VP Service Delivery, Halberd Security): Why?
[14:16] Grace Okonkwo (Chief Information Security Officer, Halberd Security): Because a tired person approving something on a phone is not a control, it's a formality.
[14:23] Tobias Lund (VP Service Delivery, Halberd Security): [pause] That's fair.
[14:26] Grace Okonkwo (Chief Information Security Officer, Halberd Security): What are they approving?
[14:28] Tobias Lund (VP Service Delivery, Halberd Security): Escalation to the client's out-of-hours contact.
[14:33] Grace Okonkwo (Chief Information Security Officer, Halberd Security): Then it's low risk and it's fine. If it were anything touching client systems I'd say no.
[14:41] Nina Patel (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): That's a useful distinction for the design. Some approvals belong on a phone and some don't, and you'd want that decided per workflow rather than as a platform setting.
[14:54] Grace Okonkwo (Chief Information Security Officer, Halberd Security): Agreed.
[14:56] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Right, I said I'd be quick and we're at fifteen minutes. Let me summarise. Renewal is agreed subject to papers — seven percent, no other changes, AI consumption estimate included. AI goes on in a contained workspace with two builders, after the fifty-incident test, subject to five written answers from Nina. And you'll introduce a publish permission separate from a build permission, once we've confirmed the mechanism.
[15:28] Grace Okonkwo (Chief Information Security Officer, Halberd Security): That's accurate.
[15:30] Tobias Lund (VP Service Delivery, Halberd Security): And the Teams approval scoping.
[15:33] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): And the Teams approval scoping, which is exploratory rather than committed.
[15:39] Grace Okonkwo (Chief Information Security Officer, Halberd Security): When do we get the written answers?
[15:42] Nina Patel (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): End of the week. If one of them takes longer I'll send four and tell you which one's outstanding rather than holding all five.
[15:52] Grace Okonkwo (Chief Information Security Officer, Halberd Security): Do that. I'd rather have four.
[15:56] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): And the renewal papers from me by Wednesday.
[16:00] Grace Okonkwo (Chief Information Security Officer, Halberd Security): Tobias will read them.
[16:02] Tobias Lund (VP Service Delivery, Halberd Security): I will read them.
[16:04] Grace Okonkwo (Chief Information Security Officer, Halberd Security): He won't read them.
[16:06] Tobias Lund (VP Service Delivery, Halberd Security): [crosstalk] [laughs] I'll read the numbers.
[16:09] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Read clause fourteen at least. It's the training one and it's the one Grace will ask you about.
[16:16] Grace Okonkwo (Chief Information Security Officer, Halberd Security): I've read clause fourteen. Three times.
[16:20] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): I know you have.
[16:22] Grace Okonkwo (Chief Information Security Officer, Halberd Security): Right. Anything else?
[16:25] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): One question, and it's for my benefit rather than yours. Eighteen months in — what's the thing that's worked best?
[16:34] Tobias Lund (VP Service Delivery, Halberd Security): The client onboarding workflow. Without question. We used to take eleven days to bring a new managed detection client live and now it's four.
[16:46] Grace Okonkwo (Chief Information Security Officer, Halberd Security): And it's consistent, which matters more than the number.
[16:51] Tobias Lund (VP Service Delivery, Halberd Security): It's consistent. That's the thing. Eleven days used to sometimes be twenty.
[16:57] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): And the worst?
[17:00] Grace Okonkwo (Chief Information Security Officer, Halberd Security): The fact that I've just found out we have no change control and version history exists that nobody's opened.
[17:08] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): [laughs] That's fair.
[17:11] Grace Okonkwo (Chief Information Security Officer, Halberd Security): It's not a criticism of the product. It's a criticism of us, and slightly of you for not mentioning it eighteen months ago.
[17:20] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): It is slightly a criticism of us. I'll take it.
[17:24] Grace Okonkwo (Chief Information Security Officer, Halberd Security): Good. Thank you both.
[17:27] Tobias Lund (VP Service Delivery, Halberd Security): Thanks. Nina, send the five.
[17:30] Nina Patel (Solutions Engineer, OrbitFlow): Four, possibly. But by Friday.
[17:33] Tobias Lund (VP Service Delivery, Halberd Security): [laughs] Bye.
[17:35] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Bye both.

question: In the churn post-mortems, what did the departing customers say OrbitFlow could have done differently?
correct_reason: The answer supports all of the required core facts and hits no penalty.

verdicts.reason: The answer quotes 'if someone had sat with two of my people for a week in the first quarter and got them to ship something real'. It does not say Kwame thinks they would still be a customer.

The answer says that when the April connector issue came up, the right response was three days of an SE building a custom connector, as the competitor did, rather than only pointing to a template or docs.
The answer quotes 'who will build the fifth workflow' and 'a proposal that includes whatever it costs to make that person real'. It does not give the 80k plus 25k example.
The answer says someone should have noticed after six months that there were four users on a thirty-user plan and said something.
The answer says Oakhill wanted a smaller plan and quotes 'five hundred a month'. It does not mention Hazel's condition about keeping approval forms.

result.question: In the churn post-mortems, what did the departing customers say OrbitFlow could have done differently?

note_fields: how the OrbitFlow team ran the call

context.text:
PER-CALL FINDINGS (each call was read on its own for this question; quotes verified)
CALL-014 (Verity Payments): They said OrbitFlow could have done several things differently: be upfront that the product still needs a person/role to build workflows, qualify who specifically would own that work, and offer hands-on implementation help much earlier. They also said OrbitFlow should have done a real integration assessment before purchase and, when the April connector issue surfaced, sent a solutions engineer to build a working custom connector instead of just pointing them to a template or docs.
   [04:56] Kwame Boateng: "if someone had sat with two of my people for a week in the first quarter and got them to ship something real"
   [05:17] Maya Chen: "We do offer that."
   [05:30] Maya Chen: "If the thing that makes the product succeed is a paid add-on"
   [09:23] Maya Chen: "That the product doesn't remove the need for the role. It changes what the role has to be good at."
   [10:03] Kwame Boateng: "You sold to my enthusiasm rather than to my capability."
   [10:31] Maya Chen: ""Name the person who'll build the second workflow.""
   [12:35] Sarah Lindqvist: "They put a solutions architect on it for three days and built us a working custom connector"
   [13:36] Maya Chen: "The right response was three days of an SE."
   [17:16] Kwame Boateng: "do the integration assessment before you buy, not after."
   [18:11] Sarah Lindqvist: "get the exported definition of a real workflow during the evaluation and have an engineer read it"
CALL-015 (Oakhill Property): Hazel said OrbitFlow could have done two main things differently: noticed after a few months that a 30-user Growth plan was being used by only four people, and offered a much smaller, cheaper plan that fit her actual needs. She also implied sales should have challenged whether the team had capacity for the roadmap rather than selling against a future that never happened.
   [05:46] Hazel Wren: "Someone should have noticed after six months that we had four users on a thirty-user plan and said something."
   [06:19] Hazel Wren: "There should be a smaller plan. Something for a company that needs five workflows and three users"
   [04:30] Hazel Wren: "Because we're two hundred and forty people and everyone's already got a job."
   [09:31] Alastair McCrae: "I probably should have pushed harder on whether you had the capacity for the roadmap we talked about."

=== CALL-014 (call kind: churn)
CALL ID: CALL-014
DATE: 2026-09-18
VENDOR: OrbitFlow
CUSTOMER: Verity Payments
INDUSTRY: Payments
COMPANY SIZE: 800 employees
STAGE: Churn post-mortem
DURATION: 21 minutes
PARTICIPANTS:
- Maya Chen, Account Executive, OrbitFlow
- Ruth Adeyemi, Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow
- Kwame Boateng, Head of Operations, Verity Payments
- Sarah Lindqvist, Engineering Manager, Verity Payments
TRANSCRIPT
[00:00] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Kwame, Sarah — thank you for doing this. You didn't have to.
[00:05] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): We nearly didn't, if I'm honest.
[00:08] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): I know. And I want to set expectations: this isn't a save attempt. You've signed with Workato, the decision's made, and I'm not going to spend twenty minutes trying to reopen it.
[00:22] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): [pause] Good. That was my concern.
[00:26] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): What I want is to understand what went wrong properly, because two years is a long time to get something wrong and I'd like to not do it again.
[00:37] Sarah Lindqvist (Engineering Manager, Verity Payments): We'll be honest then.
[00:39] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Please be.
[00:41] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): I'd add — I took over this account in January, so about eight months ago. Some of what went wrong predates me and some of it doesn't, and I'd rather you told me which is which.
[00:55] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): Alright. Where do you want to start?
[00:59] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): With the decision. When did you actually decide?
[01:04] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): Properly? June.
[01:07] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): June.
[01:09] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): Though I'd say the decision became inevitable in about February and it took us until June to admit it.
[01:17] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): February.
[01:19] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): February.
[01:21] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): That's a month after I took the account.
[01:24] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): It's not about you. I want to be clear about that.
[01:29] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): I'd still like to know what happened in February.
[01:33] Sarah Lindqvist (Engineering Manager, Verity Payments): February was when we tried to build the settlement reconciliation workflow and couldn't.
[01:40] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Couldn't, or found it hard?
[01:43] Sarah Lindqvist (Engineering Manager, Verity Payments): Couldn't, in the sense that the effort exceeded the value by a factor I couldn't justify to my team.
[01:51] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Tell me about it specifically.
[01:54] Sarah Lindqvist (Engineering Manager, Verity Payments): Our settlement provider is a mid-sized European processor. You don't have a connector for them. Nobody does, to be fair — Workato doesn't either.
[02:06] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): So what was the difference?
[02:09] Sarah Lindqvist (Engineering Manager, Verity Payments): The difference is that we ended up writing a custom integration either way, and once you've accepted you're writing custom integrations, you start asking what the platform is actually giving you.
[02:24] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): And what was the answer?
[02:26] Sarah Lindqvist (Engineering Manager, Verity Payments): Orchestration and run history, which are genuinely good. But not enough on their own for what we were paying.
[02:35] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): And this is where I'd push back on Sarah slightly.
[02:39] Sarah Lindqvist (Engineering Manager, Verity Payments): Go on.
[02:41] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): The connector gap was real. But it wasn't why we left. It was the thing we pointed at.
[02:49] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): What was the real reason?
[02:52] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): Nobody in operations ever built anything.
[02:56] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): [pause] Say more.
[02:59] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): The entire pitch — and this is the pitch I bought, so I'm implicating myself — was that my team would own their own workflows. That we'd stop queuing behind engineering. Two years in, every single production workflow was built by Sarah's team.
[03:19] Sarah Lindqvist (Engineering Manager, Verity Payments): Every one.
[03:21] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): [crosstalk] So we paid a premium for a business-user platform and used it as an engineering tool. And as an engineering tool it's fine but it's not worth the premium.
[03:34] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Why didn't your team build?
[03:37] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): [pause] A few reasons and none of them are flattering.
[03:42] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): I'd rather have unflattering.
[03:45] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): The first workflow anyone builds is hard. Not conceptually hard — fiddly. You have to understand connections, you have to understand how data moves between steps, you have to understand what happens when something's null. My operations people are good at operations. They're not good at that, and expecting them to become good at it in their spare time was naive.
[04:11] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Did you have enablement?
[04:13] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): We had a two-day onboarding at the start. Eight people attended. Six of them never touched it again.
[04:22] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): And after that?
[04:24] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): Nothing, until you arrived in January and offered some sessions.
[04:29] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): Which you declined.
[04:31] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): Which I declined, because by January I'd already half-concluded it wasn't going to work and I didn't want to spend my team's time on it.
[04:41] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): [pause] That's useful and it's painful.
[04:46] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): You asked.
[04:48] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): I did ask. What would have changed it? If I'd arrived in month three rather than month twenty?
[04:56] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): Honestly, I think if someone had sat with two of my people for a week in the first quarter and got them to ship something real, we'd still be a customer.
[05:08] Sarah Lindqvist (Engineering Manager, Verity Payments): I agree with that.
[05:10] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): Not a training course. Sitting with them. Building the actual thing they needed.
[05:17] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): We do offer that.
[05:19] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): Do you? Nobody ever offered it to me.
[05:23] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): [pause] It's a paid professional services engagement.
[05:28] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): Ah.
[05:30] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Which is possibly the problem. If the thing that makes the product succeed is a paid add-on, and the customer doesn't know they need it until it's too late —
[05:41] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): Then you've designed a product that fails by default for people like me.
[05:47] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): That's a harsher way of putting it than I would have, but I can't argue with it.
[05:53] Sarah Lindqvist (Engineering Manager, Verity Payments): Can I add the engineering perspective? Because it's different.
[05:58] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Please.
[06:00] Sarah Lindqvist (Engineering Manager, Verity Payments): My team quite liked it. The run history is genuinely better than what we'd have built. The exception queues are good. When something failed at three in the morning, we could see why, and that's not nothing.
[06:16] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): So why did you support leaving?
[06:19] Sarah Lindqvist (Engineering Manager, Verity Payments): Because we were maintaining custom integrations to a platform whose main selling point was that we wouldn't have to maintain custom integrations. And because the licence cost was being justified by a benefit — business-user autonomy — that wasn't materialising.
[06:39] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): Say the other thing.
[06:41] Sarah Lindqvist (Engineering Manager, Verity Payments): [pause] And because two of my engineers wanted to build it in-house and I spent eighteen months arguing against them, and eventually I ran out of arguments.
[06:53] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): What was your last argument?
[06:56] Sarah Lindqvist (Engineering Manager, Verity Payments): Maintenance. It's always maintenance. And it's a good argument right up until the platform also requires maintenance, at which point you're comparing two maintenance burdens and one of them costs a hundred thousand a year.
[07:13] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Is that what you're paying Workato?
[07:16] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): Less. Not dramatically less.
[07:19] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): So it isn't a price decision.
[07:22] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): It's partly a price decision, because at the margin we could justify one and not the other. But no, it's not primarily price.
[07:33] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Then what tipped it to Workato specifically?
[07:37] Sarah Lindqvist (Engineering Manager, Verity Payments): Two things. Their connector for our core banking platform is genuinely better than yours. That one's just true.
[07:47] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): It is true. We know.
[07:49] Sarah Lindqvist (Engineering Manager, Verity Payments): And their engineering-facing story is stronger. Recipes as code, better CI story, our engineers had opinions about it and the opinions were positive.
[08:02] Ruth Adeyemi (Customer Success Manager, OrbitFlow): So you've bought an engineering tool.
[08:05] Sarah Lindqvist (Engineering Manager, Verity Payments): [pause] Yes. That's fair. We've bought an engineering tool and stopped pretending.
[08:12] Kwame Boateng (Head of Operations, Verity Payments): Which is the honest conclusion. My team is never going to build workflows. That was my ambition and it was wrong, and rather than keep paying for the ambition I've accepted the reality.
[08:26] Maya Chen (Account Executive, OrbitFlow): Can I ask — do you think that ambition was wrong in principle, or wrong for Verity?
